# 170. Bedrock Credentials: API Keys vs. IAM
# Section: Building Generative AI Applications with Bedrock
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-machine-learning-engineer-associate-mla-c01/learn/lecture/57863781
# Caption: en_US (auto)

So there's a couple of ways to use Amazon Bedrock through credentials.
You can have a Bedrock API key or you can use IAM and knowing when to use one over the
other is something you got to know.
So like every other AWS service, you can use IAM to control your credentials and access to it.
And this is the preferred path for anything you're doing in production.
So if you are using Bedrock in a production application, in a production AWS workload,
this is going to give you stronger security.
It's going to inherit everything that IAM gives you through AWS authorization, and it's
built around the principle of least privilege, which is the best practice for authentication in general.
However, there is also API keys for Amazon Bedrock, and this is basically a convenience for developers.
So if you've worked with OpenAI or Anthropic, you know it's just a matter of throwing an
API key into your environment variables and you're good to go.
So if you're just experimenting, Bedrock does have the same feature.
You can just throw a Bedrock API key into your environment variables and be good.
So it's a simple bearer token style to call Bedrock API.
So if you just want to be, for example, calling Anthropic foundation models through Bedrock,
you could use a Bedrock API key to do that from your developer workstation.
Now there are two kinds of Bedrock API keys.
There are short term keys, and these just inherit the permissions of whatever IAM principle generated it.
And these are set to expire.
At the most, they can last 12 hours.
So this can be useful for short term authentication tasks.
You can also have a long term key that sticks around pretty much indefinitely, and you should
only be using these for exploration or development.
Do not use this in production.
And by all means, be careful never to check those in, right?
So never hard code a credential in your source code.
Never check them into Git just like you would with any API key.
In the short term, that limits the blast radius a little bit because they expire after a while.
Long term keys are more dangerous and you need to take care of them just like you would
with your OpenAI or your Anthropic API keys or whatever else it might be.
So again, taking a look at the diagram at the bottom here, Bedrock has two authentication mechanisms.
One is using IAM like every other service, or you can have a Bedrock API key.
And that is really intended for developer usage or quick experimentation.
For production apps, you want to be using IAM.
So that's the exam tip.
For a production AWS workload, lean toward IAM roles and temporary credentials.
If you're just doing quick experimentation as a developer with Bedrock, then an API key
might make your life a little bit easier.
But again, never hard code credentials in source code, protect them, make sure you're
not checking them in anywhere.
So standard advice there.

Let's talk a little bit about fine tuning in bedrock.
So fine tuning is basically extending the training of the underlying foundation model that you're using.
So if you need to adapt an existing large language model or maybe even an image generation model to
a specific use case, fine tuning is one way to do it, and it's a pretty good way of doing it.
I mean, you're basically training it on new data and baking that into the model itself.

You're actually enhancing the model itself with your own information.

So the good thing about the fine tuning approach, as opposed to other approaches, is that it eliminates
the need to build up this big conversation so you don't have to, like, do this big prompt engineering
exercise of including examples of your own data into the prompt itself to get the results you want.
Again, it's baked into the model itself, and in the long run that can save on tokens.
So because you don't have to keep injecting this information into the prompt since it's part of the
model in the long run, that might actually be less expensive than actually putting that into the prompt,
like you might do with prompt engineering or even with retrieval augmented generation, which we'll

However, it is expensive in the short run.

# 173. Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) - How Fine-Tuning Works
# Section: Building Generative AI Applications with Bedrock
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-machine-learning-engineer-associate-mla-c01/learn/lecture/57865475
# Caption: en_US (auto)

Let's talk a little bit more in detail about how fine-tuning works under the hood.
So a popular approach is something called LORA or Low Rank Adaptation.
It's been around for a while.
So rather than retrain the entire model from the ground up whenever you have new information
you want to train it on, it's much more efficient to just kind of slap some extra information
onto the side of the model if you would.
So what do we mean by that?
So we're going to add some what we call low rank matrices to the model at the attention layer usually.
That probably doesn't mean anything to you so let me explain that real quick.
So self-attention is kind of the breakthrough that made large language models take off a few years ago.
And there was this paper from Google called Attention is All You Need.
At a very high level the way it works is that there is this layer of these large language
models down toward the bottom that understands how the different words in your sentences
or your phrases relate to each other.
And that's how it understands the context between those words and what you're trying to do.
So that is kind of the heart of how this all works.
And by just adding a little bit more extra information to have some extra training on
that layer, it turns out we can do a pretty good job of expanding these existing models
and fine tuning them for more specific applications.
Now we might be tacking this on to other parts of the model as well.
Just attention weights is the most interesting part.
Now I'm not going to get into the math of how all this works because the exam certainly
doesn't expect you to know that.
But by low rank we're just referring to the complexity of these extra matrices that we're
slapping onto the side of the model.
Now at inference time, after we've actually trained these new matrices that we've added
into our underlying model through fine tuning, all we have to do is add these fine tuned
weights that are off on the side back into the base model.
And that's what this little diagram on the side is illustrating here.
So we have base input coming into our model at inference time.
We have the pre-trained weights from the base model.
We also have our fine tuned weights on the side there.
All we've got to do is add them together before we actually start generating the output.
So very efficient way of going about it.
The base model itself has remained unchanged.
We've just kind of tacked on some extra information onto the side that's used at inference time.
So obviously this is going to be a lot more efficient in terms of storage, training, and inference.
We don't have to go back and rebuild an entire large language model from scratch because
those things are huge.
You don't want to be paying for that.
We can just pay for these extra bits of training that we're kind of slapping onto the side there.
And the important distinction here is that I'm slapping them onto the side and not onto the top. All right.
So that's a different way of doing fine tuning.
Another approach is called an adapter layer where instead of like having these extra matrices
that are kind of alongside these different layers of the model, we just slap another
layer on top where we're kind of embedding all of our fine tuned information as sort
of an afterthought after the whole thing. That works too.
LoRa tends to work better. Okay.
So LoRa, low rank adaptation, or LoRa for short, a mechanism for fine tuning a foundation
model without discarding the whole foundation model altogether.

# 174. Catastrophic Forgetting
# Section: Building Generative AI Applications with Bedrock
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-machine-learning-engineer-associate-mla-c01/learn/lecture/57863587
# Caption: en_US (auto)

So, a very real problem you need to be aware of is something called catastrophic forgetting
when you're fine-tuning a model.
If you don't take care during fine-tuning, you can end up making your model better at
something at the expense of everything else, and that's not a good thing.
So, you need to know some techniques for avoiding that.
As an example here, let's say that I have a really good model that has not been fine-tuned
yet and it's great at coding and some basic legal tasks and it can follow instructions
and it has good general reasoning capabilities as well.
A lot of this came maybe from post-training or stuff that was specifically in the training
data set, right?
But if I then try to take that general purpose model and do heavy fine-tuning for a specific
narrow field like legal expertise, for example, that might come at the cost of everything else.
So, if I do too much fine-tuning on that narrow legal data, I might end up degrading my capabilities
for reasoning, coding, instruction following, and other topics, and you don't want that.
Now, this is most likely to happen when the new data you're fine-tuning on is very narrow
in scope or very different from the original data.
So, if you have a model that's about something and you're trying to fine-tune it for something
else entirely, that's when this can become a big issue.
The way to fix this is to mix in general data, not just the data that you're fine-tuning on.
If you're fine-tuning an Amazon Nova model, they have something called data mixing that
is specifically for this purpose.
You can also just not be quite so aggressive on the fine-tuning.
So, do it with a modest learning rate.
Do it with a modest number of epochs.
Just try not to push it too hard in that specific direction.
Otherwise, you might lose those other capabilities and experience catastrophic forgetting.
And remember, when you're evaluating your new model, don't just evaluate it on the new task.
It's very tempting to say, I'm fine-tuning this model on legal expertise, and I'm going
to evaluate how good it is on legal expertise, but you also need to evaluate what it could
do before and make sure that you did not give that up in the process, assuming it's important to you.
So, don't just evaluate what you're training it on.
Also test on the general capabilities that you don't want to lose.
And an exam tip, make sure that when you're doing customization of models through fine-tuning
or anything else, you are improving the target task without breaking everything else.
When that happens, we call that catastrophic forgetting.

# 175. Model Distillation
# Section: Building Generative AI Applications with Bedrock
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-machine-learning-engineer-associate-mla-c01/learn/lecture/57865529
# Caption: en_US (auto)

Well, let's talk about model distillation.
Kind of a hot topic these days.
A lot of the AI labs keep accusing each other of distilling their models on each other.
Kind of a way to cheat, but it can be used for legitimate purposes too.
How does it work?
Well, it's actually pretty simple.
The idea is that you're just getting responses from another foundation model and using that
to train your model.
And the idea is to take a large model and potentially use that to make a smaller model better.
So the goal is just to approach the teacher's quality for your specific workload.
So model distillation can be a way of taking the performance from a large model and just
using the bits of it that you need for what you're trying to do.
Now the idea is that the teacher will generate synthetic responses.
So you're giving it a set of prompts and capturing its responses to that set of prompts.
And then your student model will be fine tuned using the data that was generated by the teacher model.
And again, the idea here is not to steal other people's models and their work.
It's usually more legitimately to take a large model and distill that down to a smaller purpose
built model by just getting its responses on a narrow slice of what it can do.
The result can be lower inference cost and latency because you've reduced the size of
the model effectively by doing this and still retaining the task specific quality that you
want for what you've been training it on.
Now this is not the same thing as quantization or pruning.
Those are different techniques for optimizing models.
So quantization just basically compresses the amount of information that you're storing
in the actual model itself.
Pruning might be pruning layers from the model that you might not need.
Distillation is a different approach.
It's basically taking a larger model, taking its output and using that to fine tune a smaller
model rather than compressing the original.
How does this work?
So you start with a set of representative prompts.
So you need to take care in how you choose those prompts.
They need to represent what you want your new model to do, your distilled model.
You then send those prompts into your large teacher foundation model.
That teacher foundation model will hopefully produce high quality synthetic responses that
you can then turn around and use as a training data set for fine tuning on your smaller model.
And then you do that fine tuning on the smaller student model and you end up with a lower
cost lower latency specialized model that's been distilled from the behavior of the larger model.
So that's model distillation.
Basically taking one model, giving it a set of representative prompts for what you want
your smaller model to be able to do, using that output as a training data set for fine
tuning for the lower cost smaller model that specializes in what those prompts represented.
Preparing data for model distillation deserves a slide of its own.
So you need to start with a careful choice of those prompts that you're using to represent
your production workload.
So you need to think about very deeply, what do I want this distilled model to be able
to do and what kind of prompts would reflect that capability.
The formatting might also matter here too.
So if you're just doing conversations, maybe you just need JSONL conversation records of
prompts and responses.
But if you're doing something fancier like classification or agentic AI work, you might
need some more structured data on the output there that you're looking for instead.
So think about what the prompts are going to look like, what they're trying to do and
what sort of structure you need for the data that comes out of it.
The teacher will then turn your prompts into synthetic training responses.
And again, you know, the better your prompts are, the better your training data will end up being.
It all starts with your prompts.
And once you get that training data back, you need to validate that.
Make sure that it's relevant to what you're trying to do.
Don't just blindly turn around and use that for fine tuning. Check it first.
Fix and remove any bad examples and make sure you're keeping your evaluation data separate
so you can still evaluate if this model is actually getting better or worse following
that fine tuning.
Again, to break it into a diagram, we start with representative prompts, probably in JSON-L format.
Your teacher model will then generate synthetic responses.
You need to validate and clean the data that comes back somehow.
And then once you have a clean set of synthetic responses, you can use that as training data
for fine tuning your smaller distilled model.
And there are some tools available in Bedrock and Amazon for doing that.
Amazon Bedrock has a feature called model distillation, and that's why it's in this exam.
So model distillation in Bedrock will handle this for you.
Also, if you're using things at a lower level through SageMaker AI, the Nova model has capabilities
for model distillation as well.
Just remember, data preparation starts with representative prompts, so you need to start
with the prompts that's at the top of the chain here.
If you don't have the right set of prompts, you're not going to get the right training
data and you won't end up with the right distilled model.

All right, so we saw that your chunking strategy is one way to optimize the retrieval phase from
your knowledge base or retrieval augmented generation system. Another is optimizing the
actual sizes of those embedding vectors themselves. So if you recall, those embedding vectors that
we're translating our chunks of text into kind of sort of represent the meaning of those chunks
of text. More specifically, how close those vectors are to each other represents how
semantically similar these bits of text are to each other. So you need to kind of figure
out how big do those vectors really need to be. If it's too big, you're wasting space,
and you're spending money storing more information than you need to and sending more data across the
wire than is necessary, right? But if the vectors are too small, then you're going to lose some of
that important meaning, some of that important information, and it will affect the quality of
your retrieval. So smaller vectors will mean fewer dimensions per chunk, and it will cost you less to
store and process that data. But there's going to be a trade-off with your retrieval performance
there as well. Now, Titan has a default of 1024 or more dimensions. I've seen it cited as 1024 or
1536. Maybe it's changing, but it's a lot, right? So if you're storing a chunk of like 300 characters,
you might actually be spending more money storing that embedding vector than the actual chunk of
data. So ask yourself, you know, what's the size of my chunks? First of all, do I really need that
much information to encode what it means? And it might have to do with the domain that you're
dealing with as well. So depending on what kind of data you're storing, maybe it's pretty
straightforward stuff. You know, there aren't a whole lot of categories of things that might be
similar to each other. In that case, maybe you can get away with a smaller dimension size than a
larger one. So if the semantic concepts you're searching for are complex, you might benefit from
larger vector sizes in your embeddings. But if not, maybe you can experiment with smaller ones
and save a few bucks. What do I mean by sparse and dense embeddings? So this term is kind of used in
different ways, but technically a sparse vector is one that's mostly empty. That's why it's sparse.
An example is one-hot encoding. So say I have a vector that represents what kind of an animal
something is. Maybe I have a dimension for every animal I know about, and I just have a one in the
one that's actually correct and a zero in all the other ones, right? Very extreme example there,
but you know, a vector representing a chicken might just have a one in the chicken dimension
and a zero in the squid dimension and so on and so forth. And a bonobo would have a one in the
bonobo dimension, but a zero in the lemur dimension, right? So that's an example of a sparse vector.
Very similar, but obviously there's a lot of wasted space there, and that's a problem.
What you see almost all the time, like I've never seen anything but this personally, is a dense
embedding. So in the context of generative AI, typically we have these floating point dimensions
where taken together, these dimensions represent a vector in multi-dimensional space that represents
the semantic meaning of that chunk of data. This is generally what you use. Now these can be smaller,
because there's not a lot of wasted space. It's really packing that information in there, right?
That's why we call it a dense embedding vector. Now there's a trade-off here. A sparse vector is
going to give you bigger similarity factors. So you see these used a lot in recommender systems,
where we're trying to say, okay, here's the stuff this person bought, here's the stuff this other
person bought, how similar are they? And you can get some really clean similarity metrics using
those sparse vectors. But dense vectors are going to be a lot more efficient, both in memory and in
general. Now there are ways to compress sparse vectors, and we see that in recommender systems.
Kind of hard to do that on a GPU though. So you don't see that as much in generative AI.
Wait, what's a similarity factor? What do I talk about there? So a similarity factor is just some
measure of how close those vectors are. So we've talked about embeddings kind of being
close to each other, representing two things having a similar meaning. How do we actually
measure that? Well, that's what a similarity factor is. And a very common one is the cosine
similarity factor. All it is, is the cosine between those two vectors. And you can do that
in multi-dimensional space. It doesn't have to be just x and y. The math is the same. And if you
remember your trigonometry from high school, the cosine is related to the angle between the two
vectors. And it's set up in such a way that if two vectors are the same, you end up with a cosine of
one. If they're totally different, then it's a cosine of zero. So it is basically a measure of
how close those vectors are to each other in that embedding space. The other nice thing is that
cosine has a nice smoothness to it. So it doesn't just have these sharp points, you know, these

to optimize your retrieval is by embedding metadata along with your embedding vectors as well. So you

For example, in providing citations. So if I have a chunk of data, I can attach metadata saying where

# 182. Vector Stores for Bedrock: OpenSearch, S3 Vectors, Aurora pgvector
# Section: Building Generative AI Applications with Bedrock
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-machine-learning-engineer-associate-mla-c01/learn/lecture/57865597
# Caption: en_US (auto)

So, let's talk about some of the choices you have for a backend for your vector stores.
One is OpenSearch, and historically this was kind of the go-to implementation for AWS.
OpenSearch is fundamentally a serverless vector store.
It can act as one, so there is a vector index type you can use.
However, serverless does not necessarily mean scales to zero.
This is an important point in the real world.
Just because your OpenSearch instance isn't taking any traffic doesn't mean you're not
going to get billed for it. You are.
Remember to shut down your OpenSearch instances and your OpenSearch domains under the hood
if you're not using them or else you're going to keep on getting billed and they can get
pretty expensive pretty quickly.
So a word to the wise, if you're experimenting with OpenSearch as a vector store, be sure
not to just shut down OpenSearch itself, but also the underlying domains.
Now the exam historically treated OpenSearch as sort of the primary implementation for
bedrock knowledge bases.
I don't know, that could change.
Over time, there is a new S3 vectors feature we're going to talk about next, and I think
that might be sort of the new default.
Actually the new default is that it's managed for you.
So if you go to create a bedrock knowledge base today, the first option you're going
to see is a managed vector store where they kind of abstract away with the actual implementation
from you entirely.
So another choice now is that you just don't even have to think about it.
It's managed by AWS for you and it will choose.
However, you can still specify your own backend if you want to, and OpenSearch is still an option.
And OpenSearch is not limited to bedrock knowledge bases, of course, it's much more broad in what it can do.
You can also integrate OpenSearch with SageMaker AI and Hugging Face, or for custom models
that you might be using for retrieval augmented generation.
One important dial you have at your disposal here is using semantic versus hybrid search in OpenSearch.
So just straight up vector search where you're going to be comparing similarity distances
or vector distances between two different embedding vectors, that's what we call semantic.
That refers to vector search and that can be tricky because it can often be elusive
to get the relevancy that you want because it depends a lot on your chunking strategy,
the dimensions of your embedding vectors, there's a lot of ways to get that wrong.
So it can often be better to have a hybrid approach and that's going to combine both
vector and keyword search.
So that way I can get results that are similar to each other semantically, but I'm also enforcing
the presence of those keywords as well.
And that's going to require that you have filterable keyword fields indexed into your
data for that metadata to work, of course, but this is an important distinction.
So if semantic search alone based on embeddings is not enough and not giving you good enough
results, hybrid might be an answer where you get the best of both worlds of vector and keyword search.
You know, you see this on Amazon product search on the retail site, for example, if I search
for something that, you know, like a specific speaker, I might just get back a whole bunch
of speakers that have nothing to do with that actual keyword.
If you had a hybrid approach instead, I would get both those keyword matches at the top
as well as those semantic searches too.
And a newer feature is Amazon S3 vectors.
It is cheaper, a lot cheaper, up to 90% cheaper, but as we'll see, there's a trade-off.
It's also a lot simpler to use.
So all you have to do is create an S3 vector bucket, and then you can create a vector index
based on that vector bucket.
And when you create that vector index, that's when you can specify the number of dimensions
for your embedding vectors and the distance metric that you want to use for that semantic search.
And then you can just store vector embeddings using put vectors in S3, include whatever
metadata you want attached to that.
And then querying that is just a matter of calling query vectors on S3.
It's all very easy.
So as you can see in this diagram here, you have your data that you want to store in your
vector store that goes into a vector bucket.
Your vector bucket has a vector index attached to it.
And then that can talk to your knowledge bases used by Bedrock or SageMaker, or even indirectly
through open search.
And let's talk about that a little bit more.
So S3 vectors are strongly consistent.
So any data that you add will become immediately available to it.
The catch though, is that it's going to be optimized for price performance over time.
And that performance is the rub.
So S3 vectors only advertises 100 millisecond to one full second of retrieval performance.
And that's not going to be good enough for a lot of applications, right?
So what AWS recommends is a hybrid approach where you use open search for performance
critical queries, but you can fall back to S3 vectors for things that are not performance critical.
They call that a tiered search strategy.
So if you have infrequently queried vectors, maybe you put that in S3 vectors to save money,
but for things that are frequently queried, you put those in open search for better performance.
And there is connectivity between the two for that purpose.
So there's a way to copy data between S3 vectors and open search.
And well, the trick, the rub there is that you end up paying for both if you're not careful.
So that could actually end up costing you more money if you're not careful.
You can also use open search backed by S3 vectors as the engine behind it.
This works if you have an open search managed cluster in place, and that gives you the best
of both worlds open search functionality with S3 vectors as the backend.
By the way, one limit, there is a limit of 10,000 indices per bucket and 2 billion vectors
per index in S3 vectors.
Another option is Amazon Aurora, which historically was just a very simple relational database
store, but there is a PG vector extension to it that you can use to store vectors within Amazon Aurora.
This creates a new vector column type, and it can compute distances in a variety of ways
and do similarity search in a variety of ways.
And it also adds vector operations into SQL.
So even though this is a relational database kind of style thing, you can use SQL commands
to do straight up vector search.
And this can give you an advantage over open search if you need to do complex SQL style
filtering logic on top of it at all.
So that might be a little bit simpler than open search for you.
And this also has the benefit of letting you store your structured data and your vector
data in the same place.
So that same database can hold the underlying data as well as the vector embeddings for it all at once.
And this can also be appropriate for smaller medium sized RAG systems with mostly structured data.
So a single relational database, the main limitation there is that it doesn't scale
so well, but for a lot of applications, it's fine.
And the simplicity that this gives you might be preferable.
Quick side note, DynamoDB is also an option now.
So DynamoDB also has vector store and vector search capabilities.
However, I think that capability emerged too soon to the release of this exam.
So I wouldn't necessarily expect to see that on there.
However, if you do happen to see a question that rotates around DynamoDB being a valid
vector store, that actually is a choice as well.

# 184. Pre-Retrieval and Chunking Strategies
# Section: Building Generative AI Applications with Bedrock
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-machine-learning-engineer-associate-mla-c01/learn/lecture/57865669
# Caption: en_US (auto)

So what we've done so far is known as naive RAG. So we're just taking straight up RAG,
we're taking a prompt, retrieving relevant context, and augmenting our prompt to generate an answer.
Very simple, right? There are more complicated approaches though to try to improve upon that,
and we call that set of approaches advanced RAG. The idea here is that we take the R and
RAG the retrieval, and we split that up into different components. So there's a pre-retrieval
stage, and that actually refers to a couple of different things. So before we actually retrieve
a context, there's a couple of things that we can try to optimize. One is how we're indexing that
data that we're retrieving. So before we start, we have a data store somewhere, a vector database,
a graph database, some external service or system. If we think about how that data is stored and how
it's organized, that might impact the quality of the results of the context that we get back,
right? So we need to think about the data granularity, how we're chunking that data up
and storing it, and what sorts of bits of information, what the scope of that information
is that we're retrieving as the context. We can also think about what data are we indexing in the
first place. Are we missing data? Is there information that we're missing out on? Like maybe
you have PDF documents that you're extracting data from and you're only extracting the text.
What if there's information in the tables and the images in that data that you want to capture as
well? Maybe you need to be a little bit more thorough about what data you're capturing
and actually extracting before you store it in your data store. There's also the idea of query
rewriting. So that's also in the pre-retrieval state. So if I take in a query and I say,
wait a minute, this query doesn't make sense. It's asking two different things that are
completely different from each other. Or maybe it has a lot of irrelevant filler words
that don't really help matters. Maybe I need to rewrite that query to split it up into two
queries or more. Or maybe I just need to summarize that query or shrink it down a little bit to
make it easier to find relevant bits of context associated with it. Those are all in pre-retrieval.
Then we do the actual retrieval from our data store. And then we can also optimize the post
retrieval state. So do I need to massage those results that came back from the context in some
way? Do I need to winnow it down to the most relevant content before I pass it on to the
actual LLM to generate a response? So let's go into more detail on how that might work.
Let's first talk about data granularity and chunking. So when we're storing stuff into
our vector database or whatever it is, you have to ask yourself, what should I be storing in the
first place? So in our earlier example, we had blocks of lines from data, right? So whenever
data said something, we would store that entire line, which might be multiple sentences as one
bit of context, right? But the data granularity matters. So is that the right thing to do? I don't
know. Maybe we should split that up into individual sentences. I don't think so because if he's saying
something altogether, that probably represents a cohesive context that he's talking about,
but that's an example. Maybe I need to go the other way around. Maybe I shouldn't just limit
myself to data's lines. I should also include some of the lines surrounding it, the people that
he's talking to, right? That might have more information, more context of what he's saying
that might be useful in generating the answer down the road. Honestly, the only reason I didn't do
that in the earlier example was because it just resulted in too much data to process in Google
CoLab's free tier. But you need to think about that. What data am I storing? What is the granularity
of that data that's appropriate? Maybe I need to summarize those lines. So maybe instead of just
taking those lines as is, I ask an LLM, summarize this information before I store it and clean that
data up a little bit, fix any pronouns or things that might be ambiguous before we actually store
that into bits of context. So some pre-processing of that data might be useful as well. In this
example, since we're trying to recreate how data talks, rephrasing it is probably a bad idea, but
if it's just straight up information retrieval, maybe that's a good idea. You want to summarize
and compress that information before you store it. Now, the process of splitting up your data
prior to storage is sometimes referred to as chunking. So in a lot of the APIs like lang
chain and whatnot, they'll call this chunking. So that's what we need. How do we chunk up
that raw data that we're storing into bits that are relevant for contextual information?
A little bit more about chunking. So part of the idea of what we're trying to do is to make sure
we don't end up feeding more information into the LLM than it can handle. So by restricting how much
information we're storing, we're reducing the risk of passing too many tokens in the end because
our context just has too much stuff in it. So if you take this really simple, one way to do this
is to just take the input data and chunk it up into blocks of text that are within that token limit,
right? So make sure that you don't blow that limit when you're passing that on to an actual query.
And usually that's what people do. They just say, okay, I'm going to take chunks of a thousand
characters at a time or whatever it is. Maybe there's some overlap between chunks, but that's
a very naive way of going about chunking. And that's what things like lang chain do by default.
That limit is becoming larger and larger though. So it's becoming less of a constraint, but more
tokens do cost more money. So there's economic reasons to try to keep that under control as well.
Also, there's an idea of semantic chunking. So that says, okay, I'm going to chunk things up,
not just based on the length or what sentence it is, but just on the semantic
independence of its information. So this gets a little bit fancier, right? We're saying, okay,
for these lines that data said, are they similar to each other or not? And if they are similar,
maybe we'll group them together into one chunk. If they're not similar at all, we'll break that
up into separate chunks. And there's ways of measuring that the most obvious one would be
using embeddings, right? So if we take each line of data's dialogue and create an embedding,
we can have some sort of a threshold where we say, if they're less similar than this,
then we're going to split it up into separate chunks. And there's support for that in lang
chain, Lama index, and others. That's a very straightforward and common way of doing semantic
chunking. You can also use your own little standalone model like BERT or something like that
to avoid the cost of actually hitting the open AI API or something like that
and try to eliminate those costs. And you can also just ask an LLM straight up,
take this data and split it up into semantic chunks. That gets pretty costly though,
as you can imagine. Here's an example of those of what one of those prompts might look like.
If you did just throw it over to an LLM, you could say, decompose the content and pass in
all the content that you're trying to store into clear and simple propositions, blah, blah, blah.
So this is asking it to split compound sentences into simple sentences, but maintaining the original
phrasing when you can saying that if you're going to use descriptive information about a named
entity, separate that into its own distinct proposition. So try to split ideas up as much
as you can. And if there's modifiers to nouns that are required and pronouns, you want to spell those
out into what they're actually referring to so that if you end up retrieving that bit of context
out of the larger context, it still makes sense and then present the results as something we can
do something with it. Also, when we're talking about pre-retrieval, there's also the idea of
extracting data. So again, there might be more to the world than just text. If you have PDFs,
for example, or images, there are tools for extracting information from them. There's one
library called Pi PDF, and there's also some extractions in Lang chain and Lama index for
accessing structured data that might be hidden within your PDF. So if you have tables or diagrams
or charts and graphs, it's not off limits. There are tools available that will let you extract
information from them and use that as well as relevant context that you might store.
You might even just have straight up image data that's not structured at all. There's solutions
for that too. There's a package called unstructured.partition.pdf. There's also a
tool called chat doc, or you can just ask chat GPT. Hey, here's an image extract information from
it for me and have it do all the work. Again, that gets expensive, but it's an option. So those are
some of the pre-retrieval things we can do. Let's talk about some more in the next lecture.

# Section: Building Generative AI Applications with Bedrock

All right, so what are your choices for chunking in Bedrock?
How can I actually control how information is stored in a knowledge base and the granularity
of that information?
Well, you have a few choices.
So standard chunking is kind of the more straightforward approaches that aren't anything fancy.
You know, they're just based on heuristics.
So one approach is a fixed size.
So I can say, I want a certain number of tokens per chunk.
And by tokens, these are the underlying things that large language models encode words into.
So it's not necessarily true that one token equals one word, but sometimes that's usually
the case, right?
So you can sort of think of tokens as words here.
So you're going to say, how many tokens do I have in a chunk?
And also, what overlap percentage do I have?
Now the idea of overlap is that I can make sure I have a little bit of extra context
from the chunks that precede and follow that chunk, right?
So that way, I can make sure that I'm not losing some of that contextual data.
So as a very simple example here on the right, let's say that I'm chunking up the text space
the final frontier.
These are the voyages of the Starship Enterprise.
If I want a chunk size of five and an overlap of 20%, 20% of five is one token, right?
So I'm going to have five tokens per chunk, and I'm going to assume here for simplicity
that one chunk equals one word and an overlap of one chunk on either side.
So I'm going to start at the beginning space, the final frontier of these.
That's the first five chunks in that text.
Next chunk is going to be, these are the voyages of.
Because of that overlap, I'm repeating that token of these.
And then again, of the Starship Enterprise, again, repeating the overlap of the word
of from the previous chunk there.
So that's how fixed size chunking works.
In practice, you would probably have much larger chunk sizes because these individual
snippets aren't going to be semantically meaningful on their own.
Now the default setting is 300 tokens per chunk, and it also honors sentence boundaries
at the same time.
So if it needs to go a little bit bigger to preserve a complete sentence within a chunk, it will do so.
You know, you typically don't want to break up sentences if you don't have to, because
a sentence by meaning is sort of a coherent thought of some sort.
Breaking that up would be bad.
So the default chunking strategy, the default standard chunking strategy is 300 per chunk,
and I'm not going to split sentences on those chunk boundaries if I can help it.
So that's a pretty good place to start, right?
300 tokens, 300 words captures some pretty complex ideas, but we're making sure not to
make it too big, and we're also making sure not to cut off sentences in the middle.
You can also choose to have no chunking at all and just have each document that you feed
into Bedrock Knowledgebase be its own chunk.
And that gives you more control in the pre-processing stage.
So if you want to pre-process your own data however you want to, to chunk it up the way
that you want, if you output each chunk into its own document and then say, hey Bedrock,
here's a pile of documents to put into my Knowledgebase without chunking, then it will
just do whatever you gave it, and each document will be its own chunk.
So that's when you might use the no chunking option.
If you've already pre-chunked your data ahead of time into individual documents.
Now if we want to get fancier, we can do hierarchical chunking, okay?
So these are basically nested parent-child chunks where we have larger chunks that split
themselves down into smaller chunks.
And the idea here is that the initial search will hit those child chunks, right?
And that's going to give us a little bit more precision, right?
So we're going to be hitting that very specific piece of text that's relevant, hopefully,
to what the query is about.
And then to get more context, we're going to go up the tree and get more and more context
from these larger chunks of data, okay?
So the idea here is to get better precision in your retrieval from those smaller embeddings.
So smaller embeddings means more precision.
But we're going to be giving up comprehensiveness, you know, the context surrounding those little snippets.
So to reclaim that, we're going to go to these parents in the hierarchy to get that larger
context of what that little snippet is about.
So kind of a cool idea here.
On the right, you can see that kind of spelled out here.
We are just breaking down kind of the left-hand side of this tree.
So in this particular example, we have a parent chunk size of six.
So that's kind of that second level there.
We're starting off with that same larger bit of text where they're going to chunk that
up into six chunks.
And we have a child chunk size of three with an overlap of one.
And that's what this ends up looking at.
So down at the bottom child level, we have space the final with that child chunk size of three.
We have an overlap of one.
So the next chunk is going to be final frontier of these, so on and so forth.
So if we get a hit on one of those child nodes, we can then go up a level to that parent chunk
size of six and get a little bit of extra context that way.
And you can expand this to the other, you know, chunks and parent and child chunks here shown.
I only illustrated that left-hand side of the tree here, but you get the idea.
Also semantic chunking, we talked about that a little bit earlier, actually using a foundation
model to do the chunks.
So I can say, hey, foundation model, you figure out the best way to split up this information
and try to figure out how to preserve ideas within a given corpus of data instead of having
just a fixed chunk size at all.
So when you're doing this, you will specify the maximum number of tokens that you want
these chunks to be while still honoring sentence boundaries.
So you can say, hey, semantic chunker model thing, go split this up, but make sure chunks
aren't bigger than, you know, three kilobytes or whatever it is.
You can also specify a buffer size, and that's basically the number of surrounding sentences
per sentence you consider when doing these embeddings.
So for example, if I have a buffer size of one, that means for that, for every sentence
this model is looking at for semantic chunking, it will also look at the one sentence on either

# 187. Content Filtering with Amazon Bedrock Guardrails
# Section: Building Generative AI Applications with Bedrock
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-machine-learning-engineer-associate-mla-c01/learn/lecture/45286425
# Caption: en_US (auto)

Let's talk about Amazon bedrock guardrails, a very important feature for AI safety and governance and
security and all that good stuff.
Basically, it provides content filtering for both your prompts and your responses.
So for anything coming in or out of your bedrock system, whether it's a knowledge base or an agent
or whatever it is, a guardrail can make sure that people aren't saying things you don't want them to
say going into the system, and you're also filtering out the response from the system to make sure
that it's not saying anything you don't want it to say.
This works with the text foundation models currently, you know, like a Titan or Claude and whatnot.
Currently not with image models, but maybe that will change in the not too distant future.
You can filter on the word level or the topic level.
So if there's a set of things you just don't want people to talk about, you can specify either the
topics like maybe you don't want them to talk about religion or politics or whatever it might be, or
maybe you don't want them to mention your competitors.
I don't know, but you can set that all up.
You can also have it automatically filter out words and topics just based on how objectionable it might
be.
So there are various dimensions, you know, for things that are hateful or biased or whatever it might
be.
And you'll see some of those when we do a demo in a minute here.
Of course, it has a profanity filter as well that you can select, and it won't make you type all those
in yourself.
It knows what the dirty words are.
You just have to turn that on and it can also remove personally identifiable information automatically.
So if it sees anybody's phone number or Social Security number or driver's ID number or address or whatever
it might be, you can select what kinds of PII you want to remove, or you might want to mask that out.
So optionally you can just have it overlaid with sort of a in brackets address if you don't want to
print anybody's address out.
So if you want to make sure that you're not leaking any PII out of your system, that's a very good
feature to use when you're putting a guardrail on the responses from your bedrock system.
A newer feature is contextual grounding check in bedrock guardrails.
This is pretty cool.
It's intent is to help prevent hallucinations.
So it measures two things.
And you can have thresholds on these two different metrics beyond which it will filter out the result.
One is called grounding.
That's basically how similar is the response to the contextual data I received.
So if you think back to how knowledge bases and retrieval augmented generation worked, were going off
and retrieving some contextual data from a vector database, right And that will measure how similar
is the response to that sort of ground truth data that we retrieved from the vector store.
If it went off and made stuff up that wasn't in that vector store, and that documents that you actually
provided to the system, it will have a low grounding score, and you can set a threshold that says,
okay, if the response here didn't wasn't really based on what came out of the documents that I gave
it, and it kind of went off and made up its own thing based on its earlier training.
Maybe I want to filter that out.
Right.
So that's what contextual grounding check does.
It can also measure the relevance of the response to the original query.
So if it sees that the answer it gave isn't really relevant to what the original question was, you
can also use a contextual grounding check to filter that out as well.
So it's sort of a way to at least guess as to whether or not the answer you got is relevant and correct
based on the data that you gave it.
These are not perfect metrics, by the way.
So obviously grounding metrics are only going to be as good as the structure that you're storing in
your vector store.
So if your vector store has a problem where it tends to retrieve irrelevant information, this metric
won't work as well.
But it's there if you want it.
And this can be incorporated into either agents or knowledge bases.
So in both cases, you can attach a guardrail to those systems and it will automatically be applied
to all prompts and responses.
You can also configure the blocked message response so that when it does choose to filter something
out, you can control the message that the user sees.
When that happens, this will make more sense when we see an example.

# 189. Intro to Prompt Engineering
# Section: Building Generative AI Applications with Bedrock
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-machine-learning-engineer-associate-mla-c01/learn/lecture/57865719
# Caption: en_US (auto)

You know, generative AI tends to say the word delve a lot for some reason. So let's delve into
the world of prompt engineering, shall we? What is prompt engineering? Well, how you ask a generative
AI system matters a lot, right? So when you're dealing with generative AI, and chat applications
in particular, you need to ask it for what you want, and how you ask matters, the more detailed
you are, the better the more the way you ask it can really influence the result that you get. And
that's what we call prompt engineering, just the the art and science of asking the right way.
To the AI. Some of the benefits of effective prompting include boosting the model's abilities
and improving safety. So by asking things the right way, again, you can get better results
out of the model and maybe get it to do things you didn't think it could do. And if you ask just
the right way, you can also improve safety, you can prevent it from telling you to do the wrong
thing, you can tell it to not leak sensitive information, things like that, if you just make
sure you specify that in your prompt. It also allows you to augment the model with domain
knowledge and external tools without changing the model parameters or fine tuning. Now this is
getting a little bit into a gray area of what I would call prompt engineering, what they're talking
about here are specific techniques like retrieval, augmented generation, or rag for short, and LLM
agents. And I'm going to talk about that later on in the course in the context of Amazon services
for genetic generative AI, because it'll make more sense there. But what they're talking about here
is basically at a high level, taking your own documents, your own databases, your own data stores,
storing that in a very specific way that's friendly to generative AI, and then using that to
retrieve contextual information about your question, and including that in the prompt before it sends
it into the actual large language model or what have you. So in a way, it's cheating, you know,
it's taking your original prompt, looking up relevant information from an external data store,
and then combining all that together into a final prompt that's actually fed into
the model itself. When we talk about external tools, it's a similar idea, but a little bit
different. So in addition to having external information, we might have external functions
or capabilities that we introduce into the system. So we can tell through the prompt or the set of
prompts that the system has, hey, I want you to answer this question. And by the way, if you need
to figure out what the current weather is in a given city, you can use this bit of code over
here to do so. And that will allow you to access some external service to get that information.
Or if I need to like retrieve some internal information through an internal service,
here's a function you can call to actually get that information in real time. And under the hood,
the AI can actually go back and forth and say, okay, this person is asking for this information.
I have this tool at my disposal that might be useful. Let's go get some information from that
tool as well. And then combine all these responses together into a final response. Again, I'm not sure
I would call that prompt engineering, but they do lump that under this category in the AWS training
material. I'm personally going to put that off until we talk about the actual service implementation,
because I think it will make more sense. But that's what this is touching on, retrieval,
augmented generation, and LLM agents. Another benefit of effective prompting, and this is
getting back to just plain old prompt engineering, in my opinion, interacting with language models
just to grasp their full capabilities. So sometimes you just got to play around with them to figure
out what they can do, what they're good at and what they're not so good at. And obviously the
end result, what we're trying to do is achieve better quality outputs from our AI system through
better quality inputs. So garbage in, garbage out, the converse is true. If you put in a good prompt,
you're much more likely to get a good answer from a generative AI system.

# 190. Anatomy of a Prompt
# Section: Building Generative AI Applications with Bedrock
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-machine-learning-engineer-associate-mla-c01/learn/lecture/57865723
# Caption: en_US (auto)

Let's talk about how Amazon describes the anatomy of a good prompt. There are basically four
components that they talk about. The instructions, the context, the input data, and the output
indicator. Let's look at an example here. So instructions, just telling the generative AI
system what you want it to do. In this example, the instructions might be write a short dialogue
between two friends about their favorite books. Then you want to provide any relevant context
information. In this example, we might say the two friends are sitting in a cozy cafe on a rainy
afternoon. Context could also be some sort of external data that you've injected there. So
if I had some external database about examples of dialogue between two friends, maybe I could
go and retrieve some actual information about what that should be and include that as context.
Input data. In this example, we're actually providing details about those two friends to
work into the result. We're saying friend two loves fantasy novels, especially those
with dragons and magic. And friend two prefers mystery novels, especially those with clever
detectives and unexpected twists. So that's an example of input data. You could actually also
provide examples of what you want there as part of the input data. So the input data could go even
further and say, okay, for these sets of friends, here's an example of what the short dialogue might
look like. And here's another set of friends and what an example of their dialogue might look like.
And that can inform the generative AI system of the exact style that you want in the output. So
input data can be used a couple of different ways there. And finally, the output indicator,
how exactly do I want to receive the output of the system? What constraints do I want?
In this example, we're saying the dialogue should be 200 words long and should express each friend's
enthusiasm for their favorite genre. So we're giving it some guidance about how long the output
should be and what style it should be in there as well. So to recap the instructions, that's
basically the task that you're asking the large language model to do. You're providing a description
or instructions for how the model should perform. The context is any external information that can
be used to guide the model. That might be additional information about the environment in
this case, or it might be information that I retrieved from some external data store that
might be relevant to the problem. The input data is input for which you want a response.
And the output indicator is the output type or format.

---

# 192. Types of Prompts
# Section: Building Generative AI Applications with Bedrock
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-machine-learning-engineer-associate-mla-c01/learn/lecture/57865729
# Caption: en_US (auto)

There are three types of prompts you should definitely know about that Amazon covers,
and this isn't just an Amazon thing.
These are pretty widely recognized.
One is the zero-shot prompt, and this is a prompt where no examples are given.
So in the previous lesson, we gave an example of where we gave it some cases to go by of
what sentiment analysis should look like.
We gave it an example of a positive and a negative sentiment and how to label that.
You don't need to do that, though, all the time.
So if you have enough information in the training of the model itself, sometimes you don't need
to give examples at all.
You can just say, classify this as positive or negative sentiment, and it will just go off and do it.
So that just relies on the model being large enough to have enough training information
to know what you want, to actually understand what you're asking for without any explicitly
given examples handed to it.
Again, sentiment analysis being the example I want to use for that one.
You could just say, determine the sentiment of the following sentence and not give it any examples.
That would be an example of zero-shot prompting.
However, few-shot prompting is the opposite of that, where you do give it some examples.
So in a few-shot example, you could give it some examples of the desired responses to given prompts.
So you could say, again, determine the sentiment of the following sentence using these examples.
I had a great time at the park today.
Should be positive.
That restaurant had terrible service.
Should be negative.
Give it as many as you want.
The more you give it, the more you'll sort of train the system as to both examples of
what you consider to be positive and negative sentiment and also what the output should be.
So it's not only learning how to classify things through these examples that you're
giving it, it's also learning the format that you want the response in.
In this case, positive or negative.
Finally, there's chain of thought, and I mentioned this again in the previous slide, too.
If you tell it to think step-by-step, you can get it to try to break things down, break
down larger problems into their subtasks.
So an example would be describe how to solve a quadratic equation using the quadratic formula.
Think step-by-step, starting with a standard form of a quadratic equation, identifying
the coefficients, and then applying the quadratic formula.
Make sure to include an example equation and solve it.
So we've done a couple of things here.
First of all, we said think step-by-step.
That's telling it to break this down into a few subtasks.
So don't try to tackle this problem all at once.
I'm forcing you to go back and break it down into some specific subtasks here.
And often that can result in a better result and one that's more explainable as well.
I've also told it explicitly what to do.
So I'm not trusting it to do that reasoning by itself on how to break down the solving
of a quadratic equation.
I'm giving it explicit guidance on what those steps should be.
So I'm saying start with a standard form of a quadratic equation.
So it can go off and retrieve that from its training data.
Then identify the coefficients.
It can try to figure that out on its own.
Maybe it needs to write its own code to figure that out. I don't know.
And then actually apply the quadratic formula.
Again, it might go off and write some Python code to figure that out.
But we've given it guidance on how to break this complicated problem down into more straightforward subtasks.
And this is what the output of that might end up looking like in the real world.
I think this is an actual capture that I did.
So here's an example of where it actually took that example and broke it down, like
I said, and actually solved it for the specific problem.
It might have a harder time doing that if I did not tell it to think step by step.

# 194. Basics of LLM Agents
# Section: Building Generative AI Applications with Bedrock
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-machine-learning-engineer-associate-mla-c01/learn/lecture/57865755

Let's talk about agentic AI and LLM agents and a brief introduction as to what they're

One of the main challenges in AI agents is trust, so we have gateway, which lets it talk
to external services and do external tool calls, but I got to really trust that agent
before I'm going to let it go loose with my credentials and, you know, spend money and
things like that.
That's what policy is meant to address.
So policy is a more recent feature in Asian core that gives you much tighter control over
what your agents are actually allowed to do or not do and what situations are allowed to do them in.
Policies are integrated with one or more agent core gateways, so it will look at the agents
in your gateway and control what they have access to or not, and there's a little example
here on the right here.
We'll look at that in a second.
The way it works is that it intercepts all of your tool calls outside of the actual code
of your agent, and it will evaluate every one of those tool calls to make sure that
it's okay vis-a-vis your defined policy.
So let's take a look at this little code snippet on the right here.
So this is saying, for example, that if we have a refund agent and it's trying to conduct
a tool call of process refund, that's only going to be allowed if the amount of the
refund is less than $200.
So this is basically putting in a safeguard that says for a really high ticket refund,
maybe we don't want that happening automatically.
Maybe a human should look at that instead, right?
So just one simple example.
These are defined in the Cedar language, which is what you're seeing here, and Cedar is an
open source language for policy definition.
Now you don't have to learn Cedar to use this.
That's the nice part.
As you can see in the actual UI for setting up policies in the console, you can actually
construct these just using natural language queries.
So you can type in what you want and the AI model under the hood will convert that to Cedar for you.
There's also a form-based solution you can use as well if you want a little bit more
tighter control over what that Cedar language output will be.
But at the end of the day, it's a piece of code that looks like that.
And this gives you very fine-grained control.
So you can define who can do what and under what set of conditions, and this specific
example gets into all of those cases there.
So basically your agent will request an action through its tool calls, okay?
That goes through agent core gateway.
If it does go through gateway, then your policy engine can intercept those calls and then
apply your Cedar-based policies to either allow or deny those requests, right?
And then only once it passes that policy will it actually call those tools or APIs or external MCP servers.
The other thing too is that these are evaluated outside of the agent's code.
This makes them a little bit more reliable.
So you don't have to worry about whether the agent's code is going to be hiding these policies.
It's outside of that entire world.
So this is sitting external to the actual agent itself and sort of monitoring it from
the outside to make it even more reliable.
The enforcement by the way is denied by default.
So this is always a good best practice for security.
You know, you definitely want to make sure that you're just enforcing the least permissions
that you can actually get away with.
So a request comes in, if it forbids a given rule match, then it will deny it.
And if you explicitly permit it, then it will allow it.

denied by default.

mode and just use that for testing and validating your policies.
So before you actually turn them on, make sure that you're not accidentally denying
a bunch of traffic that should have went through instead.
This will make more sense when we look at it in the UI.

# 203. Handling AgentCore Failure Modes
# Section: Building Generative AI Applications with Bedrock
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-machine-learning-engineer-associate-mla-c01/learn/lecture/57865823
# Caption: en_US (auto)

Let's talk about some specific failure modes in AgentCore that you might need to know about.
They basically fall into three categories.
One is coordination failures.
So this is specific to multi-agent workflows.
One thing that can happen is that your workflow will stall or lose its state in the middle
of handing off between agents.
Some tools you can use here is storing a checkpoint state in your AgentCore memory so that you
have that information to resume from.
You can also have a timeout in place between those agents and retry them if necessary.
So this is important to make sure that those multi-agent workflows are idempotent, otherwise
those retries could be harmful, right?
So we need to make sure that it's safe to do that retry.
And you can also introduce yet another agent.
So if the problem is your agents aren't talking to each other properly, maybe the solution
is yet another agent that supervises them.
A supervisor agent could watch it and detect those stalled workers and raise the alarm
on that and try to deal with it automatically in that case.
There's also the problem of truncated streaming.
So what if I'm streaming a response back and it gets caught off in the middle?
I've seen that happen.
Well one thing you can do is make sure you're checking the stop reason to figure out why
that truncation happened in the first place.
Hopefully there's some context here that you can use in your application to retry it or
figure out what happened and get to the root cause.
And if that does happen, if you're buffering your events, it should be possible to resume
from the last chunk that you received.
If all else fails though, you can fall back to a non-streaming retry.
So if you just can't get back a streaming response in one piece, maybe you need to fall
back to a non-streaming query.
Also tool failures.
This is probably the more common case.
So you have some external tool you're calling through the gateway and it errors out or it
times out on you.
So the basic thing you can do is make sure that your tools that you have control over
are returning the information that the agent needs to deal with that error.
So don't just return an error and say, ah, I broke.
You want to return structured error information that the LLM, the agent can then act on and
find an appropriate backup or an appropriate retry mechanism.
And maybe the mechanism is to retry with exponential backoff or something like that, or apply the
circuit breaker pattern or have other tools that it can fall back on if a given tool fails on you.
Observability is the key.
You're not going to know about these failures if you're not watching for them.
So make sure you're using CloudWatch or OpenTelemetry and have alarms on error rates.
And again, keep your tools at impotence.
So if you do need to retry, that is safe to do so.

---

# 204. Other Amazon Bedrock Features (Model Evaluation, Bedrock Studio, Watermarks)
# Section: Building Generative AI Applications with Bedrock
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-machine-learning-engineer-associate-mla-c01/learn/lecture/45286455
# Caption: en_US (auto)

A few more bedrock features that we didn't talk about previously that are worth a mention.
One is that, you know, again, you're not limited to the foundation models that bedrock provides or
the custom models that you build on top of them.
You can also import your own models that were trained from scratch.
So in SageMaker you have that capability, right?
You can go off and create your own foundation model and even train your own large language model from
the ground up if you want to.
You can import that model into bedrock.
So you can either import that from SageMaker, or you can have a stored version of that model in S3
that you can import as well.
So that's just a capability that bedrock offers.
Also something worth talking about in some length is model evaluation.
So if I do build a model or if I'm trying to compare models against each other, how do I measure them?
How do I know one is better than the other?
That's actually very hard to do with generative AI because the results are so non-deterministic sometimes,
right?
How do you decide what's good?
Oftentimes it's a human decision, and that is one way to do it.
But there are automatic metrics as well.
So you can try to measure the accuracy toxicity Robustness.
There's a metric called Bert score.
You might want to remember F1, whatever it might be, and it can automatically compute those based
on test data sets that you provide of prompts and the ideal responses to those prompts, basically.
And you can either provide your own set of test prompts and responses, or there are built in prompt
data sets you can use as well that have sort of a pre-built standard test set that will measure the
relevancy of a given result from a model for a set of questions.
And some of these data sets contain questions or prompts that are specifically designed to test the
model's ability to reason things like that.
So that's one way you can evaluate models within bedrock.
Also, you can do it with humans.
So if you want to bring your own team, it provides a framework for actually evaluating your models
against human beings who are evaluating the quality of those responses.
So for example, our self reinforcement learning from human feedback is an example of that, where you
can put a couple of different responses from a model next to each other and ask humans to rate which
one is better, right?
You've probably seen that in other generative AI systems.
That's what's going on there.
It's basically human evaluation of the response from your model.
And you don't have to bring your own team either.
You can also use AWS managed teams as well, kind of like they do with Mechanical Turk.
Right?
So they have sort of this army of evaluators out there, human evaluators that you can leverage to evaluate
your model and decide whether a given response from that model is good or not.
Also, you have the ability to provide provisioned throughput.
We talked about that briefly with LM agents.
But more generally, if you want to make sure you have enough capacity for a given steady load, you
have the ability to provide provisioned throughput for the inference layer in bedrock.
Also.
One other thing is watermark detection.
So if you use the Titan Image Generation Foundation model from Amazon, it embeds a watermark into its
results that can be detected.
So if you want to take an image and determine if it was generated by that model, the flip side of that
is that there's a watermark detection module in bedrock that can be used for that purpose.
Also last thing is Bedrock Studio.
This is kind of a new feature here, at least as of this recording.
It's a web app environment.
So it's a web based workspace for bedrock that allows people to use bedrock and develop within it without
having an AWS account necessarily.
So if you want to use bedrock within an organization and you don't want to have people to have their
own AWS accounts to use it, Bedrock Studio is a way to do that from a security standpoint, uses some
sort of single sign on integration with IAM and your own identity provider.
So basically it ties together whatever sign on or account mechanism you have within your organization,
and it integrates that with IAM under the hood.
So it kind of looks like they're an AWS account under the hood.
Using Bedrock Studio, different users can collaborate on projects and also components within that project,

So good tool for collaboration within a larger environment.

# 205. Model Context Protocol (MCP)
# Section: Building Generative AI Applications with Bedrock
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-machine-learning-engineer-associate-mla-c01/learn/lecture/57865843
# Caption: en_US (auto)

An important thing in the world of agentic AI is Model Context Protocol, or MCP for short,
something Anthropic came up with a while ago, but it's really caught on. It's a standardized
interface for interactions between agents and tools, and the cool thing is that this enables
you to use external tools that are offered by third parties. So Anthropic described it originally
as a USB-C port for AI applications, so it's a standardized interface for getting context or
additional information or capabilities from external third-party systems potentially.
It doesn't have to be third-party, it could be your own as well, but it's just a standard
protocol for extending your AI agents with other stuff, you know, and what could that other stuff
be? So in this diagram on the right here, you can see that you have your AI application at the top,
it goes through the MCP layer, and that MCP protocol can front a bunch of other stuff.
Maybe it's access to data or file systems or databases locally, maybe it's development tools
locally, maybe it's productivity tools, there's tons of examples out there, but they could be
local, they could be external, I don't care, it all looks the same to MCP. Now technically the
data layer is JSON RPC 2.0, I don't think you'll have to know that, but just so you know, and the
transport layer is either standard IO for local stuff or HTTP streaming for external stuff.
So it just gives you access to external tools from your agentic AI system with a consistent
interaction pattern. So it's a standard on how apps provide context back to your foundation
model, to your LLM agentic system, and pretty much any agent SDK has model context protocol
support. MCP support is kind of a table stakes these days for these SDKs, and that
includes the strands SDK, so strands also has support for MCP baked into it. Okay, what do these servers
do? Well the way it works is that they can expose tools, resources, and prompts. So they might give
you back prompts on how to use them, and they might expose tools that you can use to extend
the capabilities of your system, or resources to provide additional context back to your system.
Okay, and just to make it real and kind of wrap your head around some examples here,
a popular one is GitHub. So GitHub has an MCP interface that will allow you to interact with
your code repository on GitHub, and do stuff as stuff's being checked in or whatever, or
getting information about repositories. So there's a common interface for that. Atlassian, if you want
a system that can automatically read your JIRA tickets, there's an MCP server for that. Postgres
QL, if you want to interact with a local database or a database within your enterprise or even
outside of your enterprise, there's an MCP server for that. There's an MCP server for Slack if you
want to integrate with Slack messages as part of your system. Google Maps, even Udemy has an MCP
server for allowing their Udemy business partners to get information about relevant Udemy courses
for a given learning path. How do you deploy your own? So this is something that definitely comes up
on the exam guide. So you got a couple of choices here, and the way they frame it is that if you're
doing something that's stateless and lightweight, something simple where there's no state you need
to maintain across different requests, they would recommend using AWS Lambda to host that MCP server
because, well, that's what Lambda's for, stateless, lightweight stuff, right? If you do need to do
something more complicated, Amazon ECS is an option, just like Bedrock Asian Core deploys
stuff to ECS, maybe your MCP server could go to ECS as well. Speaking of Asian Core, you can also
deploy MCP servers through Asian Core as well, and that's the last point on this slide, and Fargate
could be on top of that as well. It also recommends using API Gateway potentially as a way to expose
MCP endpoints, and it also encourages using MCP client libraries whenever possible to abstract
away all the complexities of the protocol. So don't reinvent the wheel if you don't need to,
obviously, right? Use client libraries. So that's the stuff that the exam guide calls out of things
you want to know about MCP. AWS also has some official MCP architecture guidance on their blog.
It's more complicated than what the exam guide and skill builder talked about, but you can see that
the guts of it are the same. So if you look over on the right there, that little dotted box that
says MCP server, you can see that we have the Fargate ECS option there, as well as Lambda's two
different options. So again, the ECS Fargate stuff for more complicated stuff, if you just have
stateless lightweight stuff, Lambda is going to be your better choice. But we've wrapped that with
authentication, Cognito, storing authentication credentials in DynamoDB, CloudWatch, potentially
ECR for managing your containers, WAF for protecting your front end, CloudFront for extending it.
So you can see you can build this whole thing around it, but the exam is really more focused
on the inner guts of it. Am I choosing ECS or Lambda for a given problem? Again, Lambda for
stateless lightweight access, ECS for more complicated stuff.
