# 206. Humans in the Loop
# Section: Building Generative AI Applications with Bedrock
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-machine-learning-engineer-associate-mla-c01/learn/lecture/57865867
# Caption: en_US (auto)

A way to extend agentic AI systems or AI systems in general is by injecting humans in the loop.
Sometimes you need a little bit of human judgment when you can't trust the API if you're doing
something more complicated.
And this can refer to any number of things, really.
So it could be as simple as just how humans consume AI generated content.
So if you are having chat GPT prepare a document for you, and then you refine the draft of
that document yourself, well, you're a human in the loop.
But usually we're talking more about workflows, right?
So you could envision a system that has an escalation criteria set into it.
So if it has a complex or uncertain thing and it detects that it's kind of going off
the rails, it might say, ah, have a human take care of this for me and route that to
a human operator somehow.
So an example would be customer service, right?
You know, if you're dealing with a customer and you're just not getting anywhere with
resolving that through the AI agent, maybe the AI agent can somehow recognize that it's
not getting somewhere and automatically escalate that to a human being for attention by filing
a ticket that goes to a human or something like that, right?
So internally it might have confidence scores or risk assessments that it's using to evaluate
that where it says, okay, the confidence of my response is not above this threshold.
So maybe I should get a human involved and actually route this to a human being to look at.
And that's where MCP integrations might come into play, right?
So that might be used to fire off a JIRA ticket or something with some external ticketing
system to get human attention on the matter.
It can also be referencing human feedback.
So just, you know, in the training and improving of models, something you've probably seen
where you're using chat GPT is sometimes it will give you two responses to choose between.
And that's an example of a human in the loop to fine tune and refine that system by injecting
your human preferences into it.
And sometimes that's a good thing.
Sometimes it's a bad thing.
You know, you might remember a period where chat GPT was really a sycophantic and really
was overly fawning over the user.
That's the result of that going sideways, by the way.
But you know, it is a valid approach.
So if you do want to collect that explicit feedback on the results and, you know, modify
your model based on that feedback and choose between different models that way, one way
of doing that is this architecture on the right here.
You could have an API gateway fronting a Lambda function that in turn goes down to DynamoDB
that stores that preference information.
So that feedback collection could be stored in DynamoDB in that situation.
And you would also need to obviously to index that in such a way that I can analyze it later on.
So this might be a good way to measure which foundation model is performing best from a
human standpoint, which variant of that model, which fine tune model is doing the best job
of making your human users happy.
So you need some way of collecting that feedback and analyzing it later.
Maybe using DynamoDB fronted by Lambda fronted by API gateway would be one way of doing that.

# 209. Evaluating LLM's with ROUGE, BLUE, and BERT scores
# Section: Building Generative AI Applications with Bedrock
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-machine-learning-engineer-associate-mla-c01/learn/lecture/57865911
# Caption: en_US (auto)

Let's talk about some specific metrics that you might use to measure a large language model and
its responses. So one is called Rouge, and that is a set of metrics for text summarization or
machine translation. And its job is to count the number of overlapping units between the computer
generated output, the output coming out of your model, and some evaluation ground truth output.
So remember, you know, one way of evaluating these models is to take its output and compare it to
some sort of set of ideal responses to your prompt. So how do we do that comparison? Rouge
is one such metric. What do you mean by a unit? That can be a word, it can be an n-gram, we'll
talk about that in a minute, or sentence fragments, however you want to slice it up.
So how similar is that generated result to the ideal result in terms of words or n-grams or
fragments of sentences? One specific type of Rouge is Rouge-n, and that's measuring the level of
overlap on n-grams, which is n is just how many words at a time am I comparing to each other.
I'll give you an example in a second here. So Rouge-1 would be based on the overlap between
unigrams, which are just one word at a time. Rouge-2 would be based on overlap of bigrams,
which are two words at a time. And then there's Rouge-L, where instead of some arbitrary number,
we're choosing the longest common subsequence between the generated and the reference text,
so whatever that works out to be. So that particular metric is good at evaluating coherence
or the order of narrative. So it actually cares about the order of the words in the response,
and that's pretty good at capturing sort of the grammar or the meaning of what you're trying to
say, right? So let's look at an example, like if you've never heard of n-grams before. Let's say
the evaluation response to a given prompt is certified AI practitioner, okay? So I can break
that phrase up into unigrams, where a unigram is one word. So there are three possible unigrams in
that phrase, certified AI and practitioner. Or I could split it up into bigrams. Bigrams are just
sets of two words that are together. So there are only two bigrams in that phrase, certified AI and
AI practitioner. So Rouge will look at the overlap between the generated output and that ideal output
in my evaluation data based on either unigrams or bigrams or whatever level of n-gram I want.
So if my model outputs certified ML practitioner instead of certified AI practitioner,
Rouge 1 would get that a score of two out of three, because two out of those three unigrams,
certified and practitioner, are common between the ideal response and the generated response. ML was
not. AI was not. Rouge-2, however, would give this a score of zero, because certified AI and AI
practitioner does not overlap at all with certified ML or ML practitioner. So based on the Rouge-1
metric here, I'm doing all right. But Rouge-2 says, no, this is terrible. And well, it kind
of is terrible because, well, these are two different exams, right? So that's an example of
Rouge. Another metric is Bleu or Bleu. I'm not sure how to pronounce that in French. That's used
more for machine translation. So the idea here is to compare the machine translation to a human
translation that's considered, again, the ground truth. This works kind of similarly to Rouge in
that it's also using engrams to do this evaluation. The difference is that Bleu is more about precision
as opposed to recall. And we'll get into that in more detail shortly. But at a high level,
precision just means we're comparing against everything, whereas recall means you're just
comparing amongst relevant results. So remember, Rouge was only looking at overlapping results
between these two data sets. Bleu looks at everything. So it's just going to check how many
words or phrases in my translation appear in my reference translation at all. You know, it's not
quite that specific. This works at the sentence by sentence level, by the way. And one other fine
point here is that it has a brevity penalty as well built into it. So if your translation is
overly short, it will be penalized for that. So, you know, can't cheat that way. Now, this does have
limited use in assessing fluency and grammar since we're going for precision over relevancy. So that
is a trade-off to keep in mind there with Bleu versus Rouge. Another metric is BERT score. And
the idea here is that we're relying on those embedding vectors we talked about earlier. So
remember, we can train a model to create these mathematical vectors associated with words or
phrases that kind of embed their underlying meaning. I'm oversimplifying, but that's the
general idea, right? So BERT score is just using those embedding vectors to compare the semantic
similarity between your output and the ideal output. Now, BERT is just a language model that
came before all the current wave of large language models. It's kind of interesting because it works
backwards from the way these other models work, but that's way too much detail for this exam.
Anyway, the fundamental thing you need to know, though, is that BERT also depends on embedding. So
that's where these embedding vectors are coming from. And because it's using embeddings and not
actual words, it's going to be less sensitive to things like synonyms or people that are
paraphrasing things because we're really trying to compare the underlying meaning of what's being
said as opposed to these specific words or phrases. So this can be a very good way of measuring
the quality of your results without depending on specific wording. So that's a more popular
metric, I would say. So that's three ways of measuring your LLM. Rouge, blue, and BERT score.

# 213. Optimizing Foundation Model Deployments
# Section: Machine Learning and AI Operations (MLOps/ AIOps) with AWS
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-machine-learning-engineer-associate-mla-c01/learn/lecture/57866041
# Caption: en_US (auto)

So we've seen how SageMaker deployments work in general and that is important information,
those blue green deployments and all that stuff, but let's get into some specific advice for
deploying foundation model deployments on SageMaker. So one thing to remember is that
SageMaker AI offers both single and multi-model endpoints. So your endpoints can actually serve
more than one model at a time, and that's one way of maximizing your resource utilization and
making sure that you're not wasting any capacity or deploying more capacity than you actually need.
So if you can repurpose the same fleet for multiple models, maybe that's a way to save
money, right? More generally, you can have multi-container endpoints. So those containers
don't necessarily have to be foundation models. They could be anything, but the point is an
endpoint doesn't have to just have one model in it. Endpoints can do more than one thing,
and that's fine. And each individual endpoint will support their own deployment guardrails,
their own VPC, and their own network isolation. Also keep in mind you can train and tune a model
in SageMaker AI. So if you want to do something a little bit fancier, like starting with a model
from Hugging Face or something and fine-tuning it, you can actually deploy that through Bedrock as
well if you don't want to deal with all the SageMaker complexity. So it is possible to use
Bedrock custom model import for that. So if you can create a model and tune it in SageMaker,
you can say, Bedrock, go grab this model from SageMaker and host that for me through a custom
model import. And now your inference is totally serverless. You don't have to think about it.
So isn't that beautiful? So that's a good way that Bedrock interoperates with SageMaker AI.
That can save you some trouble. And serverless can also be a better usage of your resources too.
Also, if you hear the term SageMaker AI inference components, that's a mouthful.
What that means is each model can get its own scaling policy. So you can actually scale each
model independently for different workloads, different use cases through SageMaker AI
inference components on the inference side with SageMaker.
Also, there are cross-region inference profiles. So if your endpoints are on Bedrock, we're going
to talk about cross-region a little bit more in a bit. But the basic idea here is that with
cross-region inference, if one specific region goes down or gets overloaded, Bedrock can automatically
redistribute that traffic to other regions. And you can restrict that traffic to a specific
geography or global. And global is actually going to give you the highest throughput.
But there are built-in features for doing that. There are some finer points. We'll get into that
later. Also, keep in mind EC2 auto-scaling groups can be used in front of SageMaker AI endpoints
that can give you load balancing and also auto-scaling, just like it says on the tin,
as a way of better managing your resources for your endpoint deployments.
And there are many ways to go about deploying a model on SageMaker AI. So you can choose from one
of many different model servers to actually host your models with. Among them are TorchServe,
if it's based on PyTorch. DJL Serving. I didn't actually, never heard of this until I actually
started studying up for this exam myself. But DJL stands for Deep Java Library. And apparently,
this is an Amazon thing, which is why you're more likely to see it on the exam. So it's basically a
Java-based deep learning library, because most things are Python these days for whatever reason.
Java's more efficient, so not a bad motivation. Anyway, with the Deep Java Library, you create
deep learning containers that you can then deploy using DJL Serving on SageMaker AI. And again,
it's an Amazon thing, but you just need to know that it's a model server that can be used with
SageMaker that serves up Java code that does deep learning. Also, it supports the Triton
inference server as well. And a few more quick points here. So another tip is to use asynchronous
inference if latency is not important. So SageMaker AI has async endpoints you can choose from if you
want to. So if you don't need an immediate response, that's a way to actually kick off
a request to your inference and then get back the result at some later point. It'll just call you
back and say, hey, I got an answer for you finally. So if you don't need, if latency is not critical,
that's the way to save a little bit of money. You could also implement yourself using SNS or SQS,
just kind of building up your own queue of hits to your inference point there and kind of like,
let them back up and control the rate that they come at. Also, there are model compression
techniques you can use to further save your inference capacity with. So smaller models
take less space to deploy and that can save you money. So some ways of doing that is quantization.
So one trick, I think DeepSeq did this, was taking an existing model and just quantizing the
bit depth of its weights down. And sometimes that works surprisingly well. So, you know,
maybe you don't need 32-bit precision for your weights, maybe 16 is enough, maybe 8 is enough
for all that matter. And that's a really great way to save some space without necessarily
losing a lot of performance. Pruning, you know, just cutting off layers in the model that you
don't need. I mean, a lot of it's unused, quite honestly. Another trick is called knowledge
distillation. And the idea here is that we train a smaller model from a larger model. So the idea
there is that we distill the useful knowledge from that larger model and force it to go into
a smaller model somehow. And, you know, it turns out that there's a lot of wasted space in some of
these larger models that you don't really need. And that's a way to kind of, well, distill it down
to what you do need. So that's a way to make a large model smaller, which means it takes less
space to deploy and will also be a little bit quicker. And general advice, do not optimize
prematurely. So it's important to always be measuring your actual performance, your actual
costs, and your actual resource utilization before you try optimizing things prematurely. Don't solve
problems that don't exist. So make sure you have monitoring frameworks set up and you're checking
CloudWatch and keeping track of what's really going on and what your real problems are and
working backwards from those problems instead of making up ones that don't actually exist.
All right. That's our general advice for optimizing foundation model deployments on SageMaker AI.

# 214. Deployment Guardrails and Shadow Tests
# Section: Machine Learning and AI Operations (MLOps/ AIOps) with AWS
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-machine-learning-engineer-associate-mla-c01/learn/lecture/45286467
# Caption: en_US (auto)

There are a few newer features in SageMaker for deployment safeguards, making sure that when you roll
out a new model, bad things don't happen.
Or if they do happen, you catch them quickly.
One is called deployment guardrails, and this can be deployed either to asynchronous or real time inference
endpoints.
I know we haven't talked about asynchronous endpoints yet, but they are what they sound like.
They're just an endpoint that gives back an asynchronous response.
So they're not waiting for a response to come back.
It just says, hey, here's a request.
Give me the answer whenever you can.
Right.
The idea here is with deployment guardrails, is that you can control the shifting of traffic to a new
model so you don't just deploy it and hope for the best.
It allows you to do something called blue green deployments.
And the idea is that your previous model is running on the blue fleet, and your new model is running
on the Green fleet.
There are three different modes of doing this.
One is called All at Once, where you shift everything over to the Green Fleet.
You monitor it for a while automatically, and if things look okay, only then will the Blue fleet be
terminated.
There's also Canary mode, where we only shift over a small portion of the traffic to the Green Fleet,
and we monitor that for a while.
Again, if that canary looks okay, then we shift everything over and then terminate the previous blue
fleet running the previous model.
There's also linear mode, where we shift traffic in linearly spaced steps.
So you can have as many steps as you want to slowly shift traffic over time to the new model and keep
an eye on it as you go.
So if you're worried about scaling or the ability of the new model to handle the traffic that you're
giving it, that's a good way to monitor things in a controlled fashion as you slowly ramp up traffic
to the new model.
And it supports automatic rollbacks.
So if things do go wrong, it can automatically roll back to the blue fleet to the previous model that
you know at least was working.
Another feature is called shadow tests, and this allows you to compare the performance of what they
call a shadow variant to production.
Very similar idea here, where the shadow variant is taking a percentage of the traffic and you monitor
its performance.
In this case you're taking a look at it manually.
You're monitoring the performance of the shadow variant in the SageMaker console, and you decide when
to promote it to production.

Even call out to Docker, tell it to build that docker file to whatever name you want to call it, and
then the code to actually invoke it would be, you know, just from SageMaker estimator, import estimator
that would invoke an estimator with an image name of whatever you specified.
So when I built that Docker image above, you see there that I called it foo.
So here I'm referring to image name foo to say I want to go load up the docker image with this name
foo, and use that as a estimator within SageMaker.
I can then call fit on that estimator to actually do the training, and we're done.
So it's just that simple.
There's a lot more detail in the SageMaker Developer Guide if you want to dig into it more, but you
probably don't need a whole lot more for the exam.
Also, I want to talk about production variance.
This is an important concept.
So you can actually test out multiple models in SageMaker on live traffic using production variants.
So there's a concept where you can have like different versions of your model.
Let's say you want to like try them out on real traffic and see how they do.
Not all models can really be evaluated offline effectively.
Recommender systems come to mind, for example, where accuracy on people's past behavior isn't always
a good indication of their performance on future unseen behavior.
So if you want to roll out a new model and test it out without taking a whole lot of risk, you could
use a production variant to actually separate those two models and run them in parallel for a while
to measure how they perform against each other.
So there's something called variant weights.
This tells SageMaker how to distribute traffic among your different production variants.
So for example, I might have a new iteration of my model and I could roll it out initially at a 10%
variant weight.
That would mean that I would be sending 90% of my traffic to the existing model, and 10% to the new
model, and I can just start ramping that up, like increase that 10% over time.
Once I gain more and more confident in its performance.
And eventually, once I'm sure that this new variant is actually doing better than the older one, I
could ramp it up to 100% and then discard the older production variant.
So this allows you to do a B tests and to validate performance in a real world setting.
Again, offline validation isn't always useful, and it's always risky to launch a new, uh, to launch
new code in general.
Right.
So this gives you a controlled way of rolling out a new model.
And if it doesn't work out well, some unforeseen problem comes out.
You can very quickly roll back to the other previous model just by changing those variant weights at
runtime

Let's delve into the world of resource management with SageMaker, making sure that you're using just
the right amount of computing power for your given algorithms.
So when it comes to choosing an instance type for a given machine learning problem, we talked about

individual algorithm there.
Technically though, that is an operations concern.
But because we spent so much time on that under modeling, that's why this particular operations section
of the course is kind of short.
We've already talked about a lot of it already.
However, there are some general tips and tricks here that you can apply.

more lightweight there and cheaper, like a compute instance or a C5.
Is the the going one.
Right now these days, and sometimes the general purpose ones, like an M5, are a good fit for training.

CPU instances that could do the same amount of work.
So even though an individual GPU instance may cost more, you're going to get more mileage out of it.
Let's also talk about managed spot training.
One cool thing you can do to reduce your costs is using EC2 spot instances for your training, and this

So if you really care about saving money and you have a very large and expensive training job, maybe

You could use spot instances to do that training and save a lot of money potentially.
The catch, of course there is a catch is that your spot instances can be interrupted at any time,
so you need to make sure you're using checkpoints to S3 so that your training can pick up where it left

Instances are in fact interrupted in that case.
So that does make things a little bit more complicated, but it can save a lot of money.
So it could be time well spent for particularly involved training jobs.
And also this can come at the cost of increasing your training time as well.
So if you need to wait for a spot instance to become available and that could be a very long wait,
right?
You have to sit around and wait for that resource to become available before your training can actually
commence.
But if what you care about the most is saving money, this can be a way to save a lot of money at the
expense of using a little bit more complexity and setting up S3 checkpoints, and at the expense of
time, because you have to wait for those resources for those spot instances to become available.
Aethes.

# Section: Machine Learning and AI Operations (MLOps/ AIOps) with AWS

And also you can use automatic scaling.

add more or fewer inference nodes to your deployment as needed.
So obviously that can save a lot of money too.
It works alongside CloudWatch to monitor the performance of your inference nodes and scale them as needed.

It's looking at individual production variants.

If you don't get that scaling policy right, You could end up not having enough capacity or having way
more than you need.
So you want to make sure that it's working good in a test environment before you actually deploy automatic
scaling into production.
One last note surrounding resource usage is the use of availability zones in SageMaker.
It's good to know that SageMaker will automatically attempt to distribute your instances across different

# 218. Token Efficiency
# Section: Machine Learning and AI Operations (MLOps/ AIOps) with AWS
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-machine-learning-engineer-associate-mla-c01/learn/lecture/57866183
# Caption: en_US (auto)

So, generally speaking, models will charge you by the token.
So, if you're looking to save money and control your costs,
trying to manage the number of tokens that are going in and out of your foundation model
is a good place to start, right?
So, before we can try to optimize our token usage, we need to measure it somehow.
And fortunately, Bedrock makes that easy.
So, there's a count tokens API in Bedrock that lets you do that.
And the beauty of it is that it will return the token count for a given request,
for a given prompt, without actually running it. And it's free.
So, if you just want to experiment with different prompts
and see how many tokens they actually use,
you can do that for free using the count tokens API.
So, you can use this in a bunch of different ways.
So, you can try testing out different models and see which ones tokenize more efficiently.
You can also do things like optimizing your prompts to fit within a given limit of tokens.
So, you can have token limits in some situations.
Maybe it's a budget that you're trying to impose on yourself.
And maybe you're just trying to use a really smaller model
that has a more fixed number of tokens available to it.
So, if you're trying to fit your prompts into a given token limit or token window,
the count tokens API is a good way of doing it.
Another tool in your tool chest is CloudWatch for this purpose.
And that can also track token usage on the output side.
So, it logs both input token count and output token count
for going in and going out of your foundation model.
And again, measuring it is the first step to optimizing it, right?
So, you can experiment with different types of applications, different kinds of prompts,
different kinds of approaches to what you're doing
and see what yields the lowest token count and therefore the lowest cost.
Now, there are other stuff that CloudWatch monitors as well
that you might find helpful for optimizing your applications.
And that includes the count of your requests and the time that they take, of course, the obvious stuff.
Also, it measures the time to first token.
So, when you're streaming responses back from a foundation model,
that time that it takes to start seeing that streaming response come back to you
is very important from a responsivity standpoint, right?
So, your application won't seem responsive if that stream doesn't start pretty soon.
And that lets you measure that.
So, that's very important from a user standpoint.
It would also log any throttles that happen, any server errors,
any client errors that happen upon invoking your models.
And at the model level, it will measure the latency, the invocation count,
and any throttling happening at the model as well.
And of course, input and output token counts as well, very important for managing your costs.
Now, there are some specific techniques for managing token efficiency that we can talk about here.
One is called context window optimization or context pruning.
These are related.
So, a lot of times the bulk of your tokens isn't coming from the prompt itself,
but by the context that you're adding into that prompt, right?
So, if you're using knowledge bases or retrieval augmented generation techniques,
those are going to be going off and retrieving a bunch of ancillary data
from some vector store or something, right?
And including that in the prompt.
And that's where a lot of those tokens are going to come from.
So, this is why it's important to have a right balance
between the size of your chunks coming back from that vector store
and the relevancy that you need.
Also, you can limit the number of chunks that you retrieve to control that cost as well.
Do you really need to be getting the top 10 chunks?
Will the top 2 do? Will the top 5 do?
That's a really big lever for managing your token efficiency.
You can also filter those chunks based on metadata.
So, we talked earlier about hybrid search techniques there,
where we're not just looking at the vector distances for your embeddings,
but also keyword search as well.
And if your keywords reveal that some of those chunks are irrelevant to the prompt,
you can toss them and save that token count as part of your contest as well.
Now, outside of RAG and knowledge bases,
another big source of token efficiency or inefficiency as it is,
is the past conversation history
or things that have been actually injected into the conversation itself,
like other documents and stuff.
So, if you're having a long conversation,
we have to keep including that past conversation history
as part of the short-term memory that's passed in along with your prompt.
That also eats up tokens.
So, what you could do is as your chat gets longer and longer and longer,
you can just start to summarize the older parts of that chat.
So, you can start to maybe safely forget about the details of it
and just have a summary that you generate
that will save on tokens going forward in that conversation.
Or maybe you just cut it off.
So, that's the idea of a context window.
We just say, okay, beyond this size,
we're just going to forget whatever was said beyond that point.
So, that might be an appropriate trade-off for you if cost is a concern.
Also, response size controls and response limiting.
So, we talked about optimizing stuff going in.
How do I optimize stuff going out?
Well, you can use a max tokens parameter on most of these models
to say, please try and get the response within this many tokens
and it will do its best to honor that.
You can also just bake that into the prompt itself if you want to
and say, respond in 50 words or less.
Of course, the irony is you're using more input tokens in that case
to try to reduce your output tokens,
so you're probably going to win in the end there.
Usually, that works too.
You can also provide some examples in your prompt
to illustrate the desired verbosity that you want.
So, if it's not as simple as saying,
fit it in this number of words or tokens,
maybe you want to give some examples of the level of detail
that you want to get back as part of the prompt
and you can use that to control the verbosity that you get back.
Also, even better, use structure data on the output side.
So, use JSON output and that will force it to use a given format
and length in its response.
Also, prompt compression is another technique.
This one's a little bit iffy.
So, the idea here is that if you do have a large chat history
or documents embedded in your prompt,
before you send that to a big expensive model,
maybe you can use a smaller model first to summarize it instead.
And this is kind of a balance, right?
Because obviously, there's going to be costs involved
in running that smaller model
and the cost of that small model needs to be less than,
you know, the cost that you would have had
by just processing it in the first place in the large model.
So, there's a balance to be struck there for sure.
But sometimes it makes sense.
Obviously, that's going to increase your latency as well.
So, now you need to wait for that small model
to do its summarization thing before it gets sent off
to the bigger model that's going to increase your latency
and make your application less responsive,
which might be a bad thing.
But, it can save on tokens.
So, if that's more important to you, go for it.
Also, if you can use knowledge bases
instead of just embedding entire documents in your prompt,
that's a win, right?
So, the whole idea of RAG and knowledge bases
is that we're just retrieving these little chunks of data
from a larger document,
not the entire document.
So, it may be tempting just to stuff an entire document
in with a prompt.
It's better to just include that in an external data store
where we can chunk it up
and just get back the relevant bits of it
and only put those relevant bits in the prompt.

# 219. Maximizing Resource Utilization and Throughput
# Section: Machine Learning and AI Operations (MLOps/ AIOps) with AWS

Yet another lever you have at your disposal for optimizing the efficiency of your system is making
sure you're maximizing your resource utilization.
So are you paying for computing capacity that's just sitting idle and not doing anything.
Well there's an opportunity if so.
One way to make sure you're eating up all that capacity efficiently and all at once is by using batching strategies.
So instead of sending individual prompts and getting back individual responses maybe I can batch
those up in some situations.
A good example is when I'm computing embedding vectors for my vector stores for my knowledge bases.
So do I really need to do that one at a time.
No that'd be crazy.
So if I have a huge document with like a huge number of chunks I want to submit those all together
in these big batches and that's going to save me a lot of money and be more efficient.
So batch up those embedding requests for vector stores.
Don't do them one at a time.
It'll be a lot faster and a lot cheaper.
Also on the inference side there is bedrock batch inference as well.
So if you don't need immediate real time responses maybe you can get away with this and also use
this to optimize the efficiency of your system.
So you can submit many prompts together stick them in an S3 bucket somewhere and say hey bedrock
batch inference go to on these and give me back all the responses together in S3 as well.
So that's going to be a much more efficient way of doing a lot of prompts at once.
Again if you don't need a real time interaction there.
Now how do I plan for capacity with bedrock.
So how do I know if I have enough resources to begin with or if I'm being throttled or I'm hitting some quota limits.
Basically you want to start by figuring out your desired tokens per minute and request per minute
that you expect your system to be able to handle.
And from there you can figure out what kind of capacity you actually need.
Now the AWS service quotas tool has within it a bedrock tool which you can see here on the right
that can help you estimate the amount of capacity that you actually need on bedrock.
And if you actually need to request a quota increase because you've exceeded the actual built in
approvals for the amount of capacity you have for bedrock.
If you do there's a form you can fill out to ask for that.
Also if you need additional capacity you can also buy provisioned throughput.
We'll talk about that in a moment as well.
Cloud formation is also an important tool for capacity planning so it does have templates that can
help you with this too.
Another thing is tensor parallelism and this is something that generally happens under the hood.
I just want you to know the term.
This is the idea of sharding a large models weights across many GPUs which any large model has to do
because they won't fit in a single GPU right.
But the end result is that we have better memory utilization per container.
So I can really say OK as I'm sharding this large model across many containers I'm really optimizing
the use of that memory on each container right.
So that's what tensor parallelism is all about.
Again something you usually don't have to think about as a application developer but the term comes up.
So I want to make sure you're familiar with it.
A little more depth on maximizing resource utilization with bedrock provisioned throughput.
So with bedrock you are allowed to provision by tokens or by model units which is a somewhat opaque
unit but it corresponds roughly to token throughput.
So if you do need dedicated capacity for deterministic performance you can do that through provision throughput with bedrock.
And you can see an example of that over here to the right.
Now if you're using a customized model you must provision throughput for that.
That is a requirement but it's generally useful for any requirement that you have for consistent
performance under high volume.
So anytime you see a scenario where you have really high performance requirements for a bedrock
model and it's not keeping up provision throughput might be the answer.
And one little fine point of this that you should know that you are provisioning for a given model
not for a bedrock overall.
And when you're actually going to use that provision throughput you need to pass through the ARN of
that specific provisioned model that you provisioned resources for.
So when you're making an actual API call for inference against that model you need to be sure to
provide the ARN for the provisioned model and not just a generic model ID for the model as a whole.
That's a very important point.
Also for utilization monitoring CloudWatch is your friend for keeping track of how you're using your resources.
It has built in dashboards as well that can be helpful for monitoring utilization monitoring.
So there are dashboards you can build with CloudWatch you don't necessarily have to use QuickSight.
Also AWS Cost Explorer is a valuable tool for attributing model costs to business functions.

Also auto scaling is an important tool in maximizing your resource utilization.
Be sure to make use of serverless solutions like Lambda, Bedrock, OpenSearch, Serverless and

You just run it and off it goes.
And you have your pre-trained model deployed to endpoints so you can hit for inference from whatever
you want.
Another way that's a little bit more complex would be using the model builder from the SageMaker Python
SDK.

is part of a larger CI CD system.
CloudFormation can be a tool for managing that and one little snippet of extra information there.
The actual name of the resource you would use for SageMaker with CloudFormation would be AWS SageMaker
model.
To specify a model that you want to host at a given SageMaker endpoint.
Few more things about inference and some of the choices you might make.
This is definitely the sort of thing that the exam loves to test you on.
So one type of inference is real time inference.
So this is often the case.
You know, you have some sort of an external application that says hey, for example maybe I got this
new person applying for a credit card.
These are the properties of that person.
Is this likely fraudulent or not?
So that would be an example of real time inference where I have an interactive workload with very low
latency requirements.
So I want to say, hey, I've got this new data I've never seen before.
I need an answer right now for this one thing, and I need it fast.
So that's an example of real time inference.
You can also use Amazon SageMaker serverless inference to do that.
So if you don't want to deal with the infrastructure that's actually running those servers that provide

And that's going to be a good choice if your workload has a lot of idle time.
So if there are periods of time where you have no traffic and you want to save money during that idle

In that instance, uh, if your traffic is more even and steady over time, it might not save you anything,

But if you have idle periods or uneven traffic, serverless might be the way to go.
You also need to be able to tolerate cold starts.
So if you do have an idle period and your serverless instance says I'm going to go to sleep for a while.

So if you have very strict latency requirements, serverless might not be the best choice.
Now, in addition to real time, you can also have asynchronous inference.
So this gives you fast latency but with a catch right.

So in that case, asynchronous inference might be the choice that allows you to provide that data very

And it will just say, okay, I'm going to go to on that for a while and process that request asynchronously
and then give you back the result when it's ready later on.
So technically that gives you near real time latency, because you can very quickly give it the data
and it will very quickly give you that data back once it's ready.
The catch there is once it's ready.
So there's two steps to that process.
You say, here's my data, I want a prediction sometime in the future and asynchronously will give you

So that's going to be appropriate for interactive workloads, but where it might take a while to generate
that result and you don't want your application sitting there blocking waiting for an answer.
Also, there are auto scaling capabilities with SageMaker inference, so you can use that to dynamically

So not quite serverless, but it's managing some of that for you.
So if you do get a sudden surge in traffic, you don't necessarily need to be woken up in the middle

And finally we should mention the use of SageMaker neo.

Foundations, and in that case, you explicitly specify the instance types that you want to test, the
traffic patterns that you expect and your requirements for latency and throughput.
And that takes longer.
That takes about two hours.
So if you want more specific results that are tailored to your specific SLAs, that might be a more
efficient way of getting there, as opposed to just looking at the the results on a whole variety of
instance types through instance recommendations and trying to make sense of that yourself.
So two different modes there, instance recommendations and endpoint recommendations.
The way to remember the endpoint recommendations are the customized load test, where you're giving
it specific requirements that it needs to adhere to.
But that's SageMaker inference Recommender, basically a tool for deciding what kind of instance types
to use for your inference endpoints and yet another way of doing it right.
So we've seen inference recommender for setting it up by hand.
We've seen serverless inference if you don't want to think about it at all.
And also automatic scaling sort of in between there.
So different ways of handling deploying capacity for your inference endpoints.

Speaking of tokens,
there are a bunch of techniques

with each turn of your conversation
and accumulating this massive context over time

Also, the retrieve context,

Some models are notorious for being overly verbose.
And unless you specifically tell it

# Section: Machine Learning and AI Operations (MLOps/ AIOps) with AWS
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-machine-learning-engineer-associate-mla-c01/learn/lecture/45286929

And let's talk about inference pipelines again.
This is the sort of thing where you just have to understand what it is and what it does for the purpose
of the exam.
So we've talked about deploying a Docker image to an inference node.
Right.
So by default you're just going to take a prepackaged image from Docker that's in ECR.
And use that to work with your trained model to do inferences at runtime.
However, you can also use more than one container and string them together using inference pipelines.
So you can have any combination of pre-trained built in algorithms or your own algorithms that are hosted
in Docker containers and hook them all together.
And you can have a linear sequence of between 2 and 15 of these containers that work together in concert.
So you can imagine combining your pre-processing, your predictions and post-processing of those predictions,
all in different containers that are chained together in an inference pipeline.
You can also use containers from spark ML or from scikit learn as part of that pipeline as well with
spark ML.
You can run that with glue or EMR, and those spark ML containers will be serialized into Emnlp format,
which is just a little piece of trivia for you there.
And you can use that for both handling real time inference and for doing batch transforms.
So your inference pipelines can be applied to either mode.
We've not talked a lot about batch transforms.
We seem to be focusing on real time inference because that's the more complicated case.
But inference pipelines can work with either usage mode.
If you're doing real time inference through a web service or batch transforms of large amounts of data
that you want to make inferences from all at once.
And that's inference pipelines in a nutshell.
It's just a way of chaining together multiple inference containers into one pipeline of results.

# 224. Model Performance Readiness and Drift Detection
# Section: Machine Learning and AI Operations (MLOps/ AIOps) with AWS
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-machine-learning-engineer-associate-mla-c01/learn/lecture/57864793
# Caption: en_US (auto)

So, let's talk about drift detection in machine learning, and this is measuring a couple of
different things.
There could be drift in the data that's going into your model, and there could be drift
in how your model is behaving over time as well.
In either case, if things start behaving unexpectedly, there might be some baseline that you're comparing
things against, and if you diverge too far from that baseline, it might be time to go
back and reevaluate if you need a new model.
So the idea is that you have some sort of a baseline that's capturing the expected or
reference behavior of your machine learning model, and then you compare production behavior
in the real world, what data is really coming in for inference, and what is my model really
putting out there, and is this diverging in time from what I expected back when I originally
trained this model.
So I can measure that on the data side, for example, by having feature distributions or
ranges or missing value rates, categorical proportions, mean, standard deviations.
The idea here is that you're measuring the characteristics of the data that you used
to train this model, and then comparing that to the characteristics of the data that's
actually being fed in for inference that it's trying to make predictions from.
And if your data that you're seeing coming in from the real world diverges too much from
what you used for training the model, that could be nature's way of telling you that
the world has changed, and maybe your model needs to change as well.
On the performance side, if you have ground truth results on what your predictions are
and how they differ from reality, you can use that to measure things like accuracy and
precision and recall and F1 score and all these other things, AUC, RMSE, MAE, whatever
it is that's appropriate for your workload.
If you do have ground truth to compare the actual performance of your model over time,
you might have a point at which you say, it's drifted too far, I need to go back and redo things.
So data on the data side, we define drift as the distribution of production inputs shifting
away from the reference or training data.
So we have a model that is consuming new data for inference, and if that data that's coming
in starts to diverge too much from the statistical qualities of the data that you used to train
the model, that might tell you that you need to go back and retrain that model.
Then there's a model quality drift.
How the actual model itself is performing is the quality of my predictions degrading
over time, and that's going to require real world labels or ground truth or human feedback
that might come later, but you got to have that to measure how good your model is really
doing and see if it's doing all right over time.
Now if your data is drifting, that doesn't automatically mean you have a problem, but
it does mean that your model is seeing data that it wasn't trained on.
Maybe your model generalizes and that's fine, but it might not.
So it's just worth a look if you see changing trends in your data that's coming into your
system versus what you trained it on.
So when you're seeing data drift, that's telling you that your input distribution changed.
Your reference is what you trained the model with, but what you're seeing in production is differing.
And then model quality drift is just saying, well, when I first deployed this model and
I measured its performance, it was at this baseline, but over time, maybe it's getting worse.
And there might be a point at which I say, I got to go back and retrain this thing or
use a different model.
How do I detect this?
So again, when you're doing your training, you have a set of reference data that you
use for training your model.
That's going to establish your baseline of what things look like on the data side.
And then on the inference side, you have inference data coming in from production, from the real world, right?
And you can compute statistics on that inference data and compare that to your baseline training data.
So over time you accumulate samples of the data that's being fed into your system from
the real world and compare its distribution to the data that was used to train your model.
If that comparison to the baseline differs using statistical tests and metrics and thresholds
that you define, you might have to go back and alert the team.
You probably don't want to automatically trigger something at that point because going back
and rebuilding that model and retraining that model is going to be a very large and
expensive task, right?
So you want a human in the loop there to make sure they make that judgment call as to whether
that's really warranted or not.
But after inspecting the upstream data and potentially retraining and re-evaluating the
model in response, you would then have to adjust all your pre-processing, replace the
model or maybe roll back a model to a previous one that worked better.
How do I do that on AWS?
So there used to be something called SageMaker Model Monitor that would do this for you.
But for reasons unknown to me, they moved that to maintenance mode.
So you cannot use that for new projects anymore.
Instead they want you to roll your own approach these days.
So there are some high level guidance they give you for how you might go about doing this.
There is open source tooling out there like MLflow apps and evidently AI.
These can be used to generate drift and model quality reports for you instead of SageMaker
Model Monitor now.
And CloudWatch might be part of the solution as well.
So if you need to publish those results somewhere where you can integrate that into your AWS
ecosystem, CloudWatch can be a place to publish those drift and quality metrics too and generate
dashboards and produce alarms that can alert people when things go out of bounds and drift too far.
QuickSight can be used for visualizing that information from CloudWatch and producing
monitoring and governance dashboards for you that can be used for monitoring drift.
And also MLflow can be used for retaining metrics and experiment model context.
And MLflow can be used for making those comparisons and also helping you conduct a root cause
analysis for why that drift is happening.
So you need to know these concepts.
You need to know the tools that you have, but you're not going to be tested on the details
that evidently are these third party open source tools.
You just need to know that given the task of model monitoring and drift monitoring,
some of the tools you might use are things like MLflow apps, evidently AI, CloudWatch and QuickSight.

# 225. Monitoring ML Models in Production
# Section: Machine Learning and AI Operations (MLOps/ AIOps) with AWS
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-machine-learning-engineer-associate-mla-c01/learn/lecture/57864801
# Caption: en_US (auto)

So what are the things that we should measure in an ML pipeline or an ML application? Well,
a lot of things. So of course there's the infrastructure itself. What am I actually
running my endpoints on and how are they healthy? Is my traffic looking like it expects to be?
Are my invocations within expected bounds? Is my latency within expected bounds?
Am I seeing a bunch of errors or failures that shouldn't be happening? These are all things to
monitor and alarm on. How's my memory utilization looking? How are my resource utilization looking
for CPU and for GPU resources? Am I throttling due to too much capacity? That's a problem, right?
Am I just saturating my resources in general? These are all things that we can monitor through
CloudWatch and set up alarms on. On the input data side, if we're training a model, am I seeing
missing or malformed features being used in that training data? If so, I should be flagging that
and looking into it. Am I seeing unexpected ranges or categories in the training data
or the data that's being sent in for inference? Again, something to watch for.
Am I seeing changes in the distribution of my input data? That can be either for training
or for inference in the real world. Am I seeing data drift in my data that's going in for inference
versus my baseline that I used to train that model on? On the output side, do my predictions match
the output distribution that I expect from my earlier testing? When I first deployed this model,
am I seeing different behavior on the whole that I'm not expecting? This is something you can
monitor. Now, in a perfect world, you would have ground truth information and I can actually
measure things like accuracy and precision and recall or F1 or RMSE, but that depends on having
ground truth data that I can actually compare my predictions against. Often that's going to be
delayed or very hard to get. So if you can get that ground truth information and actually compute
these things, obviously you want to monitor them, but you might have to make do with those output
distributions as sort of a proxy as to things behaving differently. If any of these things go
out of bounds, what do you do? Well, obviously you're going to have dashboards and alerts in
CloudWatch or what have you. And if that does actually trigger something you need to investigate,
you need to take action. So monitoring stuff doesn't do any good if you don't do anything
with the information. Go and investigate the upstream data and the infrastructure to see
what's going on. Maybe you need to retrain your model and revalidate it if things have drifted
too much over time. Maybe I need to deploy a new model version after doing that training, or maybe
it's just a matter of rolling back to an earlier model because my new one's not behaving the way
that I expected. Anyway, the monitoring is going to be workload specific. So there's no
one right way to do it. There's no specific drift threshold. There's no universal metric.
You need to kind of arrive at this through your own experimentation for every individual model
and application that you're doing. So you need to arrive at that yourself. There's no real hard
guidelines. What might this look like in production? So let's assume that I'm using SageMaker AI to
actually provide the endpoints for prediction here. My application out there in the world is going to
be hitting that AI endpoint from SageMaker to make a prediction and return those predictions
back to the user. But under the hood, SageMaker AI can be squirreling stuff away. It can be
integrated into CloudWatch and automatically monitor things for me, like the number of
invocations, latency, errors, CPU, GPU, memory, and any throttling that's happening. So that was a
whole box on the previous slide, right? SageMaker AI's integration with CloudWatch can give that to
you without a whole lot of work. And it can also capture your input and output data, or at least
sample it for you. And given that input and output data, that you can then monitor the trends in that
data over time. You can perform statistics on it to see what the distributions are and whether or
not those are drifting over time. And there are tools like MLflow and Evidently AI that are the
reference solutions that AWS gives you for doing this, because the old model monitor feature of
SageMaker has unfortunately gone into maintenance mode, but those are some third-party open source
tools you might use in its stead. Once CloudWatch is detecting something bad happening or not,
they can publish that to a dashboard and your dashboards in turn can have alarms to make sure
that you go and investigate something that's going wrong. So if something is anomalous,
it can detect that for you and wake you up if need be. You can have your own custom metrics as well.
And you might use other tools like MLflow again, or maybe QuickSight dashboards to help visualize
that data and speed up your operational flow. And that MLflow mentioned comes from the box above it
there. So this doesn't necessarily have to come from CloudWatch. That model quality analysis and
statistical analysis that you're doing as well on the capture data on the input and output side
might also be feeding into those dashboards and alarms. So MLflow might be getting data from
itself there on that model quality analysis. And if something does alarm, what do you do? Again,
check the upstream data, check the infrastructure. If you need to go back and retrain your model and
revalidate it, you might need to deploy a new model to make things better or just roll back
the model you put out that's not behaving the way that you thought.

Now, how is Docker different from a virtual machine?
Well, Docker is sort of a virtualization technology
but not exactly,
the purists will try to hit me if I say this,
so the resources are shared with a host.
That means that you can share many containers on one server.
So if you look
at the architecture for a VM, you have the infrastructure
then you have the host operating system
then you have a hypervisor
and then you have your apps and your guest operating system.
And so this is how, for example, EC2 works,
for example, when you get an EC2 machine
it is actually a virtual machine running on a hypervisor.
And so this allows Amazon to offer many EC2 instances
to many different type of customers
and all these EC2 instances
all these virtual machines are going to be separate.
They're not going to share resources
and they're going to be isolated, but for a Docker container
you still have the infrastructure and the host OS
which may be this time an EC2 instance
then you have the Docker Daemon
and then on top of it, you can have a lot
of containers that can be lightweight running
on top of the Docker Daemon.
And this allows the containers to really
cohabitate together.
They can actually share networking
share some data and so on.
So it's a bit less quote unquote,
secure as a virtual machine,
but it allows you to run more containers on a single server.
And this is why we really like Docker containers.
So how do you get started with Docker?
Well, first you have to write a Docker file,
which is defining how your Docker container will look.
So we have a base Docker image
and we add some files and then we're going to build it.
And this will become a Docker image.
And that Docker image,
you can store it on a Docker repository
it's called a Push and you push it to either Docker hub
which is a public repository, or Amazon is ECR
which is Amazon's version of Docker repositories.
Then you can pull back these images
from these repositories and then you would run them.
And when you run a Docker image
it becomes a Docker container, which runs your code
that you had built from your Docker build.
That is the whole process with Docker.

It's Amazon Elastic Container Service.
It's the own platform of Amazon for Docker management.

Then we have Amazon EKS
which is Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service
which is Amazon's managed version of Kubernetes

We'll have a quick look at it.

# 232. Amazon EKS
# Section: Machine Learning and AI Operations (MLOps/ AIOps) with AWS
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-machine-learning-engineer-associate-mla-c01/learn/lecture/45356923
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So let's talk about the other way
to run containers onto AWS, and this is using Amazon EKS.
So Amazon EKS stands for Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service.
So it is a way, as the name indicates,
to launch and manage Kubernetes cluster onto AWS.
So what is Kubernetes?
Well, this is the blue logo
you see in the top right corner of the screen.
Kubernetes is an open-source system
for automatic deployments, scaling and management
of containerized, usually Docker, applications.
So it is an alternative to ECS, which has a similar goal
which is to run your containers, but a very different API.
The idea is that ECS is definitely not open-source.
Whereas Kubernetes is open-source
and used by many different cloud providers
which gives you some sort of standardization.
So EKS supports two launch modes,
again the EC2 launch mode if you want to deploy
worker mode like EC2 instances,
or the Fargate mode if you wanted to deploy
serverless containers in an EKS cluster.
So the use case for using EKS is that your company
is already using Kubernetes on-premises,
or already using Kubernetes in another cloud,
or they just want use the Kubernetes API,
and they want to use AWS to manage the Kubernetes cluster,
then they would use Amazon EKS.
So again, Kubernetes from an exam perspective,
is cloud agnostic, it can be used into any cloud
such as Azure, Google Cloud and so on.
And so that means that if you are trying to migrate
between clouds or your containers,
using Amazon EKS may be a much more simple solution.
So in terms of diagram, this is what it looks like.
So we have a VPC, 3 AZ separated
into public subnets and private subnets.
And so you would create EKS Worker Nodes
they would be EC2 instances for example,
and each of these nodes will be running EKS Pods.
So they're very similar to ECS tasks,
but from a naming perspective,
anytime you see pods, it relates to Amazon Kubernetes, okay?
So we have EKS Pods and they're running onto EKS Nodes,
and so these nodes can be managed by an Auto Scaling group.
Now, very similarly to ECS,
if you wanted to expose EKS Service and Kubernetes Service,
we could set up a private load balancer,
or a public load balancer to talk to the web.
So let's summarize the different node types
that exist for Amazon EKS.
So you have the Manage Node Groups,
and this is AWS that will create and manage Nodes,
so EC2 instances for you.
And these nodes are part of an Auto Scaling group,
managed by the EKS service itself.
And you have support for On-Demand and Spot Instances.
You can also choose if you wanted to,
to self-manage nodes, this is if you want to have
more customizations and more control.
So in that case you need to create the nodes yourself,
and then you need to register them to an EKS cluster,
and then you manage your own nodes as part of an ASG.
You can still use the pre-built Amazon EKS Optimized AMI
for this, which saves you a bit of time,
or you can build your own AMI, which is more complicated.
This supports as well, the On-Demand and the Spot Instances.
And finally, if you don't wanna see any nodes at all,
then Amazon EKS, as I told you, supports the Fargate mode
in which there is no maintenance required,
and no nodes are managed at all you can just run containers
on top of Amazon EKS.
Now you can attach data volumes to your Amazon EKS cluster.
For this, you need to specify a StorageClass manifest
on your EKS cluster, and this leverages something called
the Container Storage Interface, CSI compliant driver.
So keywords to look out for at the exam.
And you have support for Amazon EBS,
you have support for Amazon EFS, and this is the only type
of storage class that works with Fargate.
You have Amazon FSx for Lustre
and Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP.
So that's it for Amazon EKS.

# 234. AWS Batch
# Section: Machine Learning and AI Operations (MLOps/ AIOps) with AWS
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-machine-learning-engineer-associate-mla-c01/learn/lecture/46732159
# Caption: en_US (auto)

The next service you need to know at a high level is AWS batch eight.
AWS batch allows you to run batch jobs that its name indicates, and they're based on Docker images.
And so with AWS batch you don't provision the instance.
There is a dynamic provisioning of the instances for you, whether it's an EC2 instance or a spot instance.
And batch figures out the optimal quantity and the type of these instances based on the volume of jobs
it has to do and the requirements.
So you don't need to manage any clusters.
It's a fully serverless service, just like glue, you just pay for the underlying EC2 instances that
are created by batch itself.
So you can schedule batch jobs using CloudWatch events to allow you to maybe run on a schedule.
Or you can orchestrate batch jobs using step functions.
And we'll see this in the next lecture.
But so a question you may have again is what is the difference between batch and glue.
So glue again just to go over it one more time.
It's Apache spark code Scala or Python only.
And it's focused on the ETL.
And you don't worry about configuring managing resources and you have the data catalog.
Now for batch it is a bit different.
It's for any computing job regardless of the job okay.
It's not just for ETL, it's for anything that is batch oriented.
So as long as you have a Docker image that works for batch, you can do it in batch.
So for example, a job that may be good for batch would be a cleanup task in an S3 bucket.
So you run a script on an S3 bucket to clean it up.
And you run this as a batch job every so often.
Whereas in glue it's really about taking data, transforming it, and then placing it somewhere else.
So the resources are created in your account and they're managed by batch.
So you're using EC2 instances within your account.
So you have access to all the stuff within your account.
And so if you have an ETL means you actually need to transform some data.
Glue is probably going to be a better choice.
But if you have non ETL related work but it is still batch oriented, then AWS batch will be better.
So that's it just for this service.
Hope that was helpful and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 235. AWS CloudFormation
# Section: Machine Learning and AI Operations (MLOps/ AIOps) with AWS
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-machine-learning-engineer-associate-mla-c01/learn/lecture/45356947
# Caption: en_US (manual)

Welcome to this section
on Deploying and Managing Infrastructure at Scale.
In this section, we'll see different ways
to deploy your workloads onto AWS.
And the first technology I wanna talk about
is CloudFormation.
So CloudFormation is such an important technology in the AWS
because it is a declarative way
of outlining your AWS infrastructure, for any resources,
and most of them are supported.
So to give you a concrete example,
in CloudFormation, you would say,
I want a security group.
I want two EC2 instances
that will be using that security group.
I also want an S3 bucket,
and I want a load balancer in front of all these machines.
Then CloudFormation automatically creates
all these things for you, in the right order,
with the exact configuration that you specify.
So the benefits of using CloudFormation are multiple,
but the first one
is that all your infrastructure is as code.
That means that
you will never, ever create resources manually
like we've done in this course,
which is excellent for control.
And that means that anytime you do changes
to how your AWS cloud is doing,
then it needs to be reviewed through code review,
which is a great way to operate in a cloud.
On top of things, there is a cost advantage
because each resource within the stack
is going to get a tag that is going to be similar
to all the other resources creating within the stack.
And you can also easily estimate the cost of your resources
using the CloudFormation templates.
And finally, thanks to CloudFormation,
you can have a saving strategy.
For example, you can say that in some environment
you could automate the deletion of all the templates
at 5:00 PM,
which will delete all the associated resources
with that template,
and then recreate it at 9:00 AM or 8:00 AM safely.
And so therefore, you have cost savings
because you don't have any resources
between 5:00 PM and 8:00 AM.
With CloudFormation,
it's super easy to create and delete resources,
which is one of the biggest cloud principle.
Then for productivity.
So as I said, you're able to destroy
and recreate infrastructure on the fly.
It's also generating diagrams for your templates
as we'll see very quickly.
And there's declarative programming,
so you don't need to figure out
if you need to create a DynamoDB table first,
or an EC2 instance, or all these things together.
The CloudFormation template is smart enough
to figure out how to do things.
Finally, with CloudFormation,
we don't reinvent the wheel.
So that means that we can leverage existing templates
on the web,
we can leverage documentation,
and CloudFormation supports almost all AWS resources.
That means that everything we'll see in this course
is supported by CloudFormation.
And in case it isn't,
you can use something called a custom resource
for resources that are not supported.
So CloudFormation really
is the base of infrastructure as code on AWS.
So as I said,
you can visualize a CloudFormation template
using the Infrastructure Composer service
and to (indistinct)
to visualize a WordPress CloudFormation stack.
And as you can see,
we can see all the resources
of our CloudFormation templates.
So we can see the ALB Listener,
the database security group,
the SQL database,
different security groups,
launch configuration,
application balancers, and so on.
But on top of it,
we can see the relations between all of these components
and how they're linked together,
which is very handy
when you want to understand your architecture diagrams.
So from an exam perspective,
CloudFormation is going to be used
when we have infrastructure as code,
when we need to repeat an architecture
in different environments, different regions,
or even different AWS accounts.
So that's it for me.
I will see you in the next lecture
for a short practice on CloudFormation.

# 237. AWS CDK
# Section: Machine Learning and AI Operations (MLOps/ AIOps) with AWS
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-machine-learning-engineer-associate-mla-c01/learn/lecture/45356955
# Caption: en_US (manual)

Now let's talk about
the AWS Cloud Development Kit, or CDK,
which allows you to define your cloud infrastructure
in a familiar programming language,
such as JavaScript or TypeScript, Python, Java, and .NET.
So you may be saying,
"Hey, it looks like this is overlapping with CloudFormation,
because CloudFormation we can define
the cloud infrastructure using YAML.
But now we can do it using a programming language.
So what is this?"
Well, this is something that supersedes CloudFormation,
as we'll see in a second.
So let's say we want
to define our infrastructure using TypeScript,
and so we have this code right here
in which we are defining three different things.
We are defining constructs,
and so there are high level components
that we can use thanks to the CDK.
So the first construct we're using is a VPC.
So we create a new VPC, we give it a name,
and we give it three AZs.
And this creates a VPC for us
which is going to contain some pre-made configuration.
Then we define an ECS cluster.
And the ECS cluster is named MyCluster
and has a link to the VPC we just defined.
And then we define
an application load-balanced Fargate service,
so this is a Fargate service with an ALB
which is linked to the cluster we just defined.
We define how much CPU,
how many tasks we want, so six,
the task image options, the memory limits,
and that we want a public ALB.
So all of this is defined using a programming language,
which means that if we don't have functioning code
if the code doesn't compile,
then it's going to give us an error,
and that means that our template cannot be generated.
But if the code can be compiled
because it is sound and typesafe,
then it is going to be compiled
into a CloudFormation template.
It could be either JSON and YAML.
And so therefore, we are using the CDK
to define CloudFormation templates in the backend.
But this is allowing us to be a lot more flexible about it
and use a programming language.
So that also means that we can deploy infrastructure
and application runtime code together.
So this is great for Lambda functions,
great for Docker containers in ECS or EKS.
So this is a revolution
because CloudFormation template is YAML,
it's not typesafe, you can make errors,
and you only know at the very end if it worked or not.
But with the CDK, you can define those
using constructs and a programming language.
So if you want a diagram,
then we have our application constructs.
It could be Lambda functions, DynamoDB, Amazon S3,
ECS, some step functions, and so on.
And we can use programming languages,
such as Python, TypeScript, Java, .NET.
We write our CDK file, I guess,
and then we synthesize this using the CDK CLI
into a CloudFormation template
that we will apply into CloudFormation
to define our infrastructure.
So it is a step above CloudFormation
and makes it way easier to work with CloudFormation.
So you may ask me,
what is the difference between CDK and SAM?
