# 242. AWS CodeCommit and CodeConnections
# Section: Machine Learning and AI Operations (MLOps/ AIOps) with AWS
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-machine-learning-engineer-associate-mla-c01/learn/lecture/57864209
# Caption: en_US (auto)

Really quick, let's talk about CodeCommit and CodeConnections, two tightly related technologies.
They're both source control, version control systems.
Kind of a good story here.
They actually tried deprecating CodeCommit at one point and there was this big uproar
from the developers and said, no, we want it back.
So they brought it back.
And as a result, it's back in the exam guide for this exam.
What CodeCommit is, is a AWS hosted Git repository, which is of course a version control system.
It's a private Git repository and it has all the AWS stuff surrounding it, like IAM
and integration with other services.
But what made it special is that this can act as the source stage for a code pipeline.
So if you had a continuous integration, continuous deployment pipeline built in AWS, you could
set things up so that if you do a Git push into CodeCommit, that could automatically
trigger your pipeline for CICD.
So I could push updated training code for machine learning, and then a pipeline could
kick off to actually retrain my data using that training code and redeploy the model automatically.
So the pipeline would look very simply like this, CodeCommit gets a push or something.
That code change can then trigger a pipeline through CodePipeline to do whatever the heck you want.
Now, when they tried to deprecate CodeCommit, what they wanted to do was push people toward
CodeConnections.
And CodeConnections is just a connection between AWS and third party Git repositories.
So if you want to use an existing Git repo, as opposed to CodeCommit, then you can use
CodeConnections to do that.
So that can connect to GitHub, GitHub Enterprise, GitLab, or Bitbucket.
And from that point, it kind of works the same way as CodeCommit.
So if you have CodeConnections hooked up, you can actually see those commits into your
third party repository, and then trigger a code pipeline that way as well.
So in this world, you have some external repository running on GitHub or GitLab or Bitbucket.
CodeConnections monitors that, and then that can trigger your code pipeline for doing continuous
integration and continuous deployment.
So CodeCommit is AWS hosted GitHub, CodeConnections, basically external Git repositories or whatever it might be.
But they both serve the same purpose of integrating your code commits into a code pipeline for
CI, CD under AWS.

---

# 243. CI/CD for AI Artifacts
# Section: Machine Learning and AI Operations (MLOps/ AIOps) with AWS
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-machine-learning-engineer-associate-mla-c01/learn/lecture/57864387
# Caption: en_US (auto)

Let's talk about how continuous integration and deployment applies to AI artifacts.
It's really not much different from code, except that the artifacts themselves are different, right?
So, and they might be stored in version in different places.
So in AI, we have version artifacts beyond just the source code of the application itself.
We have things like prompt templates and prompt versions, and those might be managed by Amazon
Bedrock Prompt Management, potentially.
We have the models themselves.
If you're deploying actual models that you've tuned or trained yourself, you might be storing
those and versioning them in SageMaker Model Registry and MLflow.
If you're using agents and developing agents and configuring them, you might be using Bedrock
Agent Core for that.
Versions and aliases under that, and when we talk about Bedrock Agents, by default,
we're talking Agent Core these days, not the Bedrock Agent Classic product that's been
put into maintenance mode.
Also knowledge bases and their configuration for retrieval.
Those might also be versioned alongside your app as well.
So whether it's source code for your actual application itself, prompt templates and versions,
the actual machine learning models and custom foundation models you might have, your agents
and the configuration for those agents, and your knowledge bases configurations.
These are all different artifacts that are specific to AI, but from a CI, CD standpoint,
it's treated just like code.
Now every one of these artifacts, just like code, will have its own version history and
its own registry that your pipeline can pull from.
So just like code, you're going to handle these AI artifacts as part of your deployment pipeline.
Code pipeline or code build can orchestrate builds and automate your tests and run evaluations
and deployments too.
Now a quick note here, it is important that you're not allowing your AI system to manage
this whole thing itself.
You don't want your AI system controlling its own tests and writing its own test code
and writing its own evaluations because it could cheat.
You know, it could say, oh, okay, I'm just going to loosen up this test because I'm not
passing it and that way I can pass it.
So it's important to make sure that those tests and evaluations are things that you
wrote and that they're sitting outside of where the AI can actually reach them.
Now once you actually do have something tested, only the approved and registered versions
that result are going to be promoted to production.
Otherwise you're going to kick it back and try again.
And you know, you're going to build them, package your stuff up, run your tests and evaluations.
If it passes, you're going to register it and version it and then push it out.
And if something goes horribly wrong, you can have a mechanism hopefully to roll back
to an earlier known good version if they actually got that far.
Ideally that test and evaluation phase would have caught it though, right?
So CICD and the whole concept of AI ops isn't really all that different from traditional
CICD for pushing out applications.
It's just that the artifacts are different.
You're not limited to code.
You have these other artifacts for AI in the mix as well.

---

# 244. Automating RAG Updates
# Section: Machine Learning and AI Operations (MLOps/ AIOps) with AWS
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-machine-learning-engineer-associate-mla-c01/learn/lecture/57864515
# Caption: en_US (auto)

Another AI-specific pipeline to think about is dealing with changes in your knowledge base.
So when your source documents change, what happens?
You need to go and compute new embeddings and store them again in your vector store
somehow automatically, right?
So there's a real challenge to keeping your retrieval index in sync with your source documents
over time, or else they'll start to drift, and that's a bad thing.
So if you're doing retrieval augmented generation and using a knowledge base of some sort, there
is a real problem here of keeping that data and those vectors in sync with what's in your
source documents if those source documents change over time.
Now Bedrock Knowledge Bases does have a feature to help you with this.
There's a start ingestion job API you can call to automatically reprocess new data.
So it can handle the ingestion and the sync for you once you call that, but something
needs to call that, right?
So there still needs to be some sort of a pipeline around ingesting this data that you're
kicking off with that start ingestion job call.
And that can reprocess anything that's been added, modified, or deleted from your source
data automatically if you've set it up right.
Now you can do this as an event-driven process as well.
So you could set things up so that it's automatically monitoring your data in S3 or something, and
whenever something changes, it can automatically kick off that ingestion job, or it can run on a schedule.
You can just say, you know, start it up every night for looking for anything that's new.
But however you're triggering it, you need to make sure you're checking the status of
that job when it's done and validating the retrieval before you promote it to actual
usage in a production setting.
So a pipeline might look like this.
Your source documents change.
Maybe you call start ingestion job on your Bedrock knowledge base to handle this automatically,
or maybe you have some other system of your own, but something needs to ingest those changes,
preprocess them, and chunk them up.
And that's going to involve updating the embedding vectors for anything that's new or changed.
Then you have to store those somewhere, right?
So you need to update the underlying vector store or knowledge base with those new embedding
vectors that represent the meaning of each chunk of data alongside with some way of retrieving
the original data itself.
And then we need to make sure it worked.
So validate that your retrieval quality is still good, and we didn't break something in the process.
Only at that point should you promote things to production and promote your new knowledge
base into production use.
So this is another example of sort of a continuous integration and deployment pipeline that's
specific to retrieval augmented generation and knowledge base updates.
Exam tip, just remember that you can only consider a refresh of your knowledge base
successful once your ingestion completes and you verify that your retrieval quality is still good.

---

# 245. Prompt / GenAI Regression Testing in CI/CD
# Section: Machine Learning and AI Operations (MLOps/ AIOps) with AWS
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-machine-learning-engineer-associate-mla-c01/learn/lecture/57864521
# Caption: en_US (auto)

Let's talk more specifically about continuous integration and deployment with generative
AI applications and regression testing with them because it is sort of a different beast.
Unlike a lot of software, these things are not deterministic, right?
So different runs might produce varying responses even between runs with the same model or the same prompt.
So it's not quite as straightforward to measure if something's working the way you expect
because it's non-deterministic.
All you can do is try to measure and judge the quality of the output against some sort
of criteria you have, you need some sort of a threshold there as opposed to exact string
or numerical matches on the output.
So that's how life is a little bit different when you're doing regression testing on generative AI.
The trick is to maintain a fixed evaluation data set or a fixed prompt data set and then
running that evaluation data set across your new prompt or your new model whenever it changes.
And these evaluations should cover normal cases, edge cases, and the key business scenarios
that you care about just like with any other testing that you might be doing, right?
Now optionally, you can also have ground truth responses.
So if you do have sort of what the ideal response to a prompt would be given a given prompt
or a given model, you can use that to measure how close the output was to that response.
But again, you can't do an exact string match, you just have to say, well, how close semantically
was my answer to what I think is the correct answer here?
And that's something you can measure.
It is important to keep a held out test set just like you would with trained test and
machine learning, right?
So you want to make sure that the data you're testing against was not used for optimizing
the prompt or the model that you're testing.
So it's a very big problem, right?
When people run evaluations on models, they run these tests on them that the model was trained on.
So you want to make sure that your test was not part of your training data set with generative
AI systems and foundation models, just like you would with any other machine learning model.
So conceptually, you have a change to a prompt that you want to test, you have a change to
a model you want to test, you have some evaluation data set that you're going to run against
that prompt or model, your set of evaluation prompts that you're going to use for testing purposes.
You will then score and evaluate the responses from that evaluation set of prompts.
And again, it can't be a hard test, it can just be measuring the semantic similarity
basically between those and what do you expect to see.
If it passes your thresholds, again, it's not going to be an exact match, you have to
have a threshold in place, only then will you deploy the prompt or model to production.
And if it doesn't pass those thresholds and a human has to take a look at it, you're going
to have to go back and revise your prop, revise your model that you're testing and rerun the
evaluation again.
Or maybe there's something wrong with your evaluation that you need to dig in as well. You never know.
More concretely though, so again, you need to run your candidate prompts or models against
some evaluation data set.
And how do I do that evaluation?
So there are many things I can measure there.
So when I'm measuring what I got out of a model versus what I expected to get, you can
measure correctness, you can measure completeness, you can measure relevance, you can measure safety.
Is it actually, you know, telling me things that aren't exposing personal data and stuff like that.
And there might be some criteria of your own that's specific to the task that you're trying to do.
Whatever it is, you have to set an acceptance threshold so that your pipeline can block
deployment when your quality meaningfully regresses from that threshold.
So you're going to have some measure or multiple measures of how good the results are and automatically
block deployment if you're not meeting those thresholds.
Now Bedrock Model Evaluations has a lot of tools that helps you do this.
So there's a bunch of different models you can pick from within Bedrock Model Evaluations
if you're using Bedrock.
So there's a large suite of built-in metrics like correctness, completeness, relevance,
and a bunch and bunch of other stuff that you can choose from there.
You can also have your own custom metrics.
So if you do have task specific criteria like we talked about, you can integrate those into
Bedrock Model Evaluations as well.
Tested evaluation is also an option too.
So you might have an army of humans out there that's actually applying their own judgment
as to how well the results are.
Sometimes that's all you can do.
If it's something that's truly subjective, maybe you just have to get this model in front
of some test subjects and see what they think about it.
Have them do a little bit of A to B testing on it before you deploy it more widely.
Or you can use another model as a judge.
So this is a very popular technique.
If I just want to gauge the quality of this output, maybe a different model can be the
judge of that other model's output.
And they can give me a measure of how good that response is in the eyes of this other model.
And ideally, that will be a completely different model from a different family of models so
that you don't have sort of a bias of one model evaluating itself, if you will.
Make sure they have different training data sets and come from someplace else ideally.
For the exam, the important point is that when you're doing regression testing on generative
AI applications, you can't just do hard equations.
You can't just say, is this the expected output?
The best you can do is have thresholds because it's going to be more of a qualitative evaluation
due to the non-deterministic nature of how these models behave.

# 247. Gitflow, GitHub Flow
# Section: Machine Learning and AI Operations (MLOps/ AIOps) with AWS
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-machine-learning-engineer-associate-mla-c01/learn/lecture/45286955
# Caption: en_US (auto)

So we've seen the mechanics of how git works.
How do you actually use it in the real world?
What are some processes you might use to manage the flow of fixes throughout your source code?
Well, kind of the old fashioned way of doing it is git flow, and this is still widely used.
This diagram on the right here illustrating it was generated by Atlassian, which is a popular tool
in the world of scrum.
And honestly, I mean, the complexity of this has always been a turnoff to me.
Like the idea is that you have a lot of different branches going on.
So you have a main master branch, which is your current release that's in production.
That's easy enough to understand, right?
But then you might also have a develop branch, and that's going to be keeping track of any changes
since the last release to Main or Master.
In addition, you might have feature branches off on the side that are being used for developing specific
features over time.
And you might have release branches that are used to merge changes with the development branch that
correspond to releases that ultimately go to production.
And then you might also have hotfix branches that are being branched off of main for urgent fixes that
need to be done right away that don't have these larger processes around features or longer term development.
And as you can imagine, keeping all these things in sync and merging them can become a little bit of
a nightmare.
But that's what git flow is all about.
That's what we call that workflow there.
And there's a little bit of a example here of how that might work.
You can see we have color coded branches here for master and a hotfix there that's being done off of
master.
We have a develop branch that's kind of for longer term development.
That's kind of steadily going along there and purple.
And then we have feature releases that are branching off of development for specific feature work.
Again, it's a good way to compartmentalize things, but it gets really complicated.
So kind of what's in style these days is what we call GitHub flow.
And with GitHub flow there are only two branches.
There's the main master branch and then you have feature branches and that's it.
So if you have a new feature you want to work on, maybe that's, you know, something urgent, maybe
it is a bug fix.
You just make a feature branch to deal with that.
And once you've tested that work, you merge it back to main.
And the key here is that this only works if you're able to deploy that to production immediately.
So you don't want things getting out of sync.
We had all these different branches before to let you work in parallel on multiple things, but if you're
integrating these changes immediately, then that problem goes away.
But that's the catch right?
So GitHub flow only works if you have the ability to release quickly.
So that implies that you have a suite of automated tests and deployments that can be run quickly and
automatically, and maybe the ability to even release multiple times per day as new features are being
checked in.
So the simplicity of this arrangement depends on your agility, your ability to actually get this stuff
out quickly.
So you've heard the expression move fast and break things.
Well, that's kind of what GitHub flow enables.
So whether that's a good thing or not, it's up to you.
So there are trade offs here right.
The old fashioned way if you will, of git flow allows you to do more stuff in parallel.
But it does come at the cost of more complexity.
GitHub flow is simpler, but it does imply that you're releasing things very, very frequently and well,
for some applications that might not be appropriate.

# 250. AWS Step Functions
# Section: Machine Learning and AI Operations (MLOps/ AIOps) with AWS
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-machine-learning-engineer-associate-mla-c01/learn/lecture/45286959
# Caption: en_US (auto)

Let's do a high level overview of AWS step functions, very similar to data pipelines and concept here.
Basically, it's a purpose in life is to let you design workflows throughout AWS.
So as you're building a system to analyze your data and pre-process that data, step functions might
be what connects all those steps together to create a larger system.
It also lets you visualize these workflows very easily, as we'll see shortly.
It generates these nice little graphs that show you the order that things actually execute within.
And it also has an advanced error handling mechanism and a retry mechanism that lives outside of the
code that you're actually running within your AWS step function.
So that's a good utility for being able to manage portions of your workflow that don't work.
You know, you don't have to rely on the code of each step actually being able to monitor itself.
AWS Step Functions can take a look at it from the outside and deal with errors when things don't do
what they're supposed to do.
It also maintains an audit history of all the workflows that have run, so you can go back and see what
happened historically if you need to troubleshoot something, it allows you to wait an arbitrary amount
of time between steps.
So if you just want to place some time in between these steps and, you know, sync up with some business
workflow that you have, you can do that.
And the maximum execution time of a given state machine that's a given workflow is one year.
So you can actually define a workflow that spans an entire year if you want to.
Can't imagine a situation where you need to do that, but if you need to, it can handle very long lived
processes and workflows.
The syntax of how it all works really is not important.
They're defined using the JSON based Amazon States language or ASL.
The exam will not expect you to be able to parse or write this kind of code, or know ASL.
You just need to know what it does.
So as long as you know what step functions are for and some examples of what you might use it for,
that's what's important for the exam.
So we're going to go through a few examples of how you might use step functions in the real world.
Here's an example of using it to train a machine learning model.
So you can see that when we start we generate the data set.
In this example, it's doing that by kicking off a Lambda function.
It then trains the model using SageMaker XGBoost algorithm.
And when it's done, it saves that trained model from SageMaker and applies a batch transform to that
model from some data set that we had at that point.
It's done.
So you can see here we've, uh, automated the entire process of generating our data training a machine
learning model, using that data, saving that trained model, and then applying data to that trained
model all in one set of steps here that are managed through step functions.
We can also use it to tune a machine learning model.
So in this example we're generating a training data set.

# 251. AWS Step Functions: State Machines and States
# Section: Machine Learning and AI Operations (MLOps/ AIOps) with AWS
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-machine-learning-engineer-associate-mla-c01/learn/lecture/45286975
# Caption: en_US (auto)

Let's go into a little bit more depth on AWS Step Functions, because this is a very powerful orchestration
tool and it's extremely relevant to data engineering.
So you can expect a lot of questions on this in the exam.
First some terminology.
So the workflow that you're defining in your step functions is called a state machine.
That's just a fancy way of saying we have some system that defines a bunch of states that your data
pipeline might be in, and it moves between those states somehow based on some criteria, right?
Every step in that workflow is called a state because it's part of a state machine, right?
That's it.
Just some terminology, just some words.
However, there are many different types of states that you can use with AWS step functions.
So it is important to know these.
The most useful one is the task state.
So that is a state within your step function state machine that does something right.
Maybe it kicks off a lambda function.
Maybe it kicks off some other AWS service to transform your data, or move it around, or load it or
whatever it needs to do.
Maybe it even talks to third party APIs to do something external to AWS.
In any case, that's a task node.
It's performing some sort of real operation on your data as you go.
There's also a choice state, and this adds conditional logic through choice rules.
These can be things like comparisons.
You know, if my data is bigger than this amount, maybe I do something special with it.
If this data contains PII or something, maybe I do something special with it, right?
So choice states are just a opportunity to apply conditional logic.
There's also a wait state that can be used to delay the state machine for some specific amount of time.
If you, just for whatever reason, want to give things, you know, time to catch up, kind of a hacky
way to do it, but you can bake in a time delay into your step functions as well with a wait state.
There's also the parallel state, and this allows you to do separate things in parallel and separate
branches of execution.
So a parallel state isn't well, it's kind of a blurry concept of state, right.
It's really saying I'm going to create many states running in parallel at this point going on so I can
have different things happening at the same time once I hit a parallel state.
Now there's also the map state, so this can get confusing.
This is something you should probably remember So a map is also run in parallel.
But it says I'm going to run this following set of steps for each item in a data set Dataset in parallel.
So this is especially relevant to data engineering because it's specifically made for operating on data.
It's going to be able to work with JSON files, S3 objects, CSV files, whatever you might have, but
it's going to take a set of steps and apply those to that data set in parallel.
So remember, a map operation will split things up into parallel processing on your data, just like
Apache Spark might or anything else, and it will run in parallel without needing a separate parallel
state in front of it.
It's a parallel implicitely.
Okay, so a little bit of confusing there.
Between parallel and map states, their parallel is used for kicking off separate branches within your
state machine that can do whatever.
But Map is specifically about operating on your data in a parallel way.
Finally, there's pass, succeed and fail.
Pass just passes your data along to the next step.
It's usually just used for debugging.
Succeed and fail or where you're going to end up.
So once you're done with your state machine, you either succeed with that state machine or fail.
And that's how you kind of wrap things up.
So that's step functions in a bit more detail there.
Do you remember what the valid types of states are and what they do?
It might come in handy.

# 256. Principle of Least Privilege
# Section: Security, Identity, and Compliance
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-machine-learning-engineer-associate-mla-c01/learn/lecture/45286997
# Caption: en_US (auto)

Let's dive into security, identity and compliance.
This is a quick one.
We're going to start off with a very basic principle of security, but an important one the principle
of least privilege.
And the exam guide does say you need to know what this is.
It's pretty simple though.
All it means is that you're only granting the permissions required for someone to perform a given task.
So it's kind of common sense, right?
Don't give people more permissions than they need to do what they need to do.
Otherwise they might figure out a way to exploit or abuse that extraneous permission that they have.
Now, while you're developing, it certainly makes sense to start with broader permissions, since you
don't necessarily know exactly what you need permission for when you're still building a system and
figuring out what components make it up right.
But once you're done, once you actually know what somebody needs to do with that system, you should
lock it down.
Once you have that better idea of the exact services and operations that a workload requires over on
the right here, we have an example of that.
So this is just an IAM policy that restricts S3 access to listing a specific bucket.
And furthermore within a specific prefix of that bucket.
So that top half there is saying I'm only going to allow list bucket operations within my specific bucket
under the data reports path there.
And for actually reading data, the only thing I'm going to allow with this IAM policy is reading CSV
files that are under my specific bucket slash data slash reports and end with a dot csv suffix.
So if you have, for example, a workflow that requires people to or a system or a service to read CSV
files from a specific location, there's no reason to give them access to anything more than that location,
and furthermore, just to the specific types of files that they might need from that location.
Right?
So that's an example of the principle of least privilege.
And if you're not sure what privileges you need for an operation, you can use a tool called the IAM
Access Analyzer.
And that will automatically generate least privilege policies based on the actual observed access activity.
So if while you're testing your system, you're only doing what you're supposed to do, you could use
IAM Access Analyzer to automatically give you a starting point of what those least privileged policies
might look like.

to actually allow your training and hosting to work.
So remember, if you disable internet access from your notebooks, you're going to have to set up Privatelink
or a Nat gateway to make sure that you can get through your VPC to get the outbound connections that
you need for training and hosting to work.
Also, your training and inference containers are also internet enabled by default.
It is possible to enable network isolation on those as well.
But again, you're going to lose S3 access by doing so, so you'll have to work around that somehow.
Um, you know, it is a security concern in general that SageMaker has to get to S3 still somehow.
So you can tighten that up using these techniques, but you still have to make sure that SageMaker has
the S3 access that it needs.
We mentioned using IAM with SageMaker, the identity and access management service.
Here are a list of some of the specific permissions you can set that are related to SageMaker.
So you can set a specific permissions for creating training jobs, creating models, creating endpoints.
Creating hyperparameter tuning jobs, creating notebooks.
You can lock these down or enable them to whatever degree makes sense for a given user.
So if I want a user that I just want to be able to create notebooks but not actually deploy them, or
create notebooks, but not actually create a huge training job that might cost a lot of money.
Or I might just want to lock down hyperparameter tuning jobs because those in particular can get really
expensive.
You can do that through user permissions with IAM and SageMaker.
There are also some predefined policies you can use, such as SageMaker read only access, SageMaker
full Access administrator access, and a data scientist policy as well that you can use just out of
the box.
A brief mention of logging and monitoring again.
So again, it's a good practice to use CloudWatch.
In general, CloudWatch can log, monitor and alarm on your endpoints for actually doing inferences,
and it can monitor the invocations of those endpoints and the latency of those endpoints as well.
Very important for runtime performance, right?
The health of the nodes themselves, the CPU available memory, things like that can also be monitored.
And you can also use CloudWatch with ground truth which is kind of neat.
So if I want to monitor how many active human beings, how many workers are actually working on my job
and how much work they're doing, I can actually monitor that as well through CloudWatch.
So kind of an interesting twist there.
You usually think of CloudWatch as monitoring machines, but it can monitor the performance of humans
doing your labeling tasks as well.
And CloudTrail is again used for auditing.
So that's going to record actions from your users roles and services.
Within SageMaker, the log files containing that log information are delivered to S3, where they can
later be used for auditing purposes

# 262. IAM Policies
# Section: Security, Identity, and Compliance

# Caption: en_US (manual)

Okay, so now let's discuss, IAM policies in depth.
So let's imagine we have a group of developers,
Alice, Bob and Charles, and we,
attach a policy at the group level.
In that case, the policy will get applied
to every single member of the group
so both Alice, Bob, and Charles
they will all get access and inherit this policy.
Now, if you have a second group with operations
with a different policy,
David and Edward will have a different policy
than the group of developers.
If Fred is a user,
it has the possibility not to belong to a group.
And we have the possibility to create what's called
an inline policy which has a policy
that's only attached to a user.
So that user could or could not belong to a group
you can have inline policies for whatever user you want.
And finally, if Charles and David both belong
to the audit team and you attach a policy to the audit team
as well, Charles and David will also inherit
that policy from the audit team.
So in this case, Charles has a policy from developers
and a policy from audit team.
And David has a policy from audit team
and a policy from the operations team.
That should make a lot of sense
when we get into the hands-on.
Now, in terms of the policy structure,
you just need to know at a high level how it works,
as well as how it is named.
So this is something you will see quite a lot in AWS,
so get familiar with this structure
this is adjacent documents.
And so an IAM policy structure, consists of a
version number, so usually it's 2012-10-17,
this is the policy language version.
And ID which is how to identify that policy,
this is optional.
And then more statements,
and statements can be one or multiple ones,
and a statement has some very important parts.
So the Sid is a statement ID, which is an identifier
for the statement, which is optional as well,
so on the right hand side is the number one.
The effect of the policy itself, so it is whether or not
the statement allows or denies access to certain API,
so in the right hand side, this says allow,
but you can see deny as well.
The principle consists of which accounts, user or role
which, to which this policy will be applied to.
So in this example, it's applied to the root accounts
of your AWS accounts.
Action is the list of API calls that will be
either denied or allowed based on the effect.
And the resource is a list of resources,
to which the actions will be applied to.
So in this example, it is a bucket,
but it could be many different things.
And finally in, not represented here
but there's a condition to which when
this statement should be applied or not,
and this is not representative here because it is optional.
So going into the exam, you need to make sure
that you really understand the effect, the principle,
the action and resource, but don't worry,
you will see those along the way in the course
so you should be confident with them
by the end of the course.
That's it for this lecture, I hope you liked it.

# 264. IAM MFA
# Section: Security, Identity, and Compliance
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-machine-learning-engineer-associate-mla-c01/learn/lecture/45357017
# Caption: en_US (manual)

Now that we have created users in groups,
it is time for us to protect these users
in groups from being compromised.
So for this, we have two defense mechanisms.
The first one is to define
what's called a password policy.
Why?
Well, because the stronger the password you use,
the more security for your accounts.
So in AWS you can set up a password policy
with different options.
The first one is you can set a minimum
password length and you can
require specific character types.
For example, you may want
to have an uppercase letter, lowercase letter,
number, non alphanumeric characters,
for example, a question mark and so on.
Then you can allow or not IAM users
to change their own passwords,
or you can require users to change their password
after some time to make your password expired,
for example, to say every 90 days,
users have to change their passwords.
Finally, you can also prevent password reuse
so that users, when they change their passwords,
don't change it to the one
that they already have or change it
to the one they had before.
So this is great.
A password policy really is helpful
against brute force attacks on your account.
But there's a second defense mechanism
that you need to know going into the exam.
And this is the Multi-Factor Authentication or MFA.
It is possible, you already used it
on some websites, but on AWS it's a must
and it's very recommended to use it.
So users have access to your account
and they can possibly do a lot of things,
especially if they're administrators.
They can change configuration,
delete resources and other things.
So you absolutely want to protect
at least your root account and hopefully,
all your IAM users.
So how do we protect them on top of the password?
Well, you use an MFA device.
So what is MFA?
MFA is using the combination of a password
that you know and a security device that you own.
And these two things together
have a much greater security
than just a password.
So for example, let's take Alice.
Alice knows her password,
but she also has an MFA generating token.
And by using these things together
while logging in, she's going to be able
to do a successful login on MFA.
So the benefit of MFA is that even if Alice
has lost her password
because it's stolen or it's hacked,
the account will not be compromised
because the hacker will need to also get a hold
of the physical device of Alice,
that could be her phone, for example,
to do a login.
Obviously that is much less likely.
So what are the MFA devices option in AWS?

# 268. Encryption 101
# Section: Security, Identity, and Compliance
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-machine-learning-engineer-associate-mla-c01/learn/lecture/45357043
# Caption: en_US (manual)

Okay, so in this lecture,
if you're not too familiar with how encryption works,
I want to give you a little bit of details
on how it works at a high level.
So, first let's talk about encryption in flight,
which is going to be referred as TLS or SSL.
TLS is the newest version of SSL.
So what we have is that the data is going to be encrypted
before sending the data.
And then it will be decrypted after receiving it.
So this is for communication
between a client and a server over a network.
And so what's going to be happening
is that for encrypting the data
TLS certificates are going to be used.
And this is what you see when you go onto websites
and it says HTTPS, that means that the connection
between you and the server
is going to be encrypted using TLS certificates.
Why do we want encryption in flight?
Well, because we're sending data over a network
and sometimes a public network
and the data goes around many different servers.
We don't want to be having a man in the middle attacks
where a middle server receives the data
and just observes the packages we're sending to the server.
And so what we want to have HTTPS or TLS, or SSL,
this is when we know that only the target server
can decrypt the encrypted data we're sending.
So let's take an example.
We have a client and a server
and we want to be able to securely login
into the server by providing our username and password.
But we only want the target server to be able to receive it.
So we're going to have the username and password
and then we're going to apply TLS encryption
on the client side automatically.
The data is going to be encrypted and sent over the network.
So as you can see, no between server can decrypt the data
and only the target server
can use the TLS decryption mechanism
to decrypt that package
and then see that we've sent the username and password.
And therefore say that we're securely logged in.
So that's for encryption in flight.
The next one is around the server side encryption at rest.
The idea is that the data will be encrypted
after being received by the server
so that it's stored securely.
And then it will be decrypted
before being sent back to our clients.
It will be stored in an encrypted form
thanks to a key, and that key is usually a data key.
And so the whole idea of managing these keys
for encryption and decryption
is that the management must happen somewhere
and the server must have access to these keys.
So let's take a service,
for example, Amazon S3.
We're sending an object over HTTP,
maybe even HTTPS for inflight encryption.
And so the service receives our object, but it is decrypted.
So the service can use a data key,
and using the data key and the decrypted objects,
we can have encryption of that object at rest.
And then when it comes to sending back that object
to the clients, the encrypted objects and the data key
will be used together to decrypt.
We'll have a decrypted form of object,
and then that object will be sent over HTTPS
back to the clients.
So we received the decrypted object as is.
As we can see in this case,
there is a server side encryption
because all the encryption and decryption
happens on the server.
So finally let's talk about client-side encryption.
And the idea is that this time
the data is encrypted and decrypted at the client side.
And the server should never be able to decrypt the data
because we don't trust a server in that case.
So for this, we could leverage encryption
for this mechanism.
So let's have an example.
The client has an object
and the data key this time is client side.
And after encryption, we get an encrypted object.
That encrypted object can be sent then securely
to any storage service available, an FTP server,
Amazon S3, EBS volumes, et cetera.
And they will be stored in encrypted form.
So the entire server can not even decrypt the data contents.
When we retrieve the contents,
we retrieve the encrypted object directly.
And if we still have access to the data key client-site,
then we're able to perform the decryption mechanism
and get the decrypted objects back.
So that's it for the three encryption mechanisms
we can see in the Cloud.
I hope you liked it.
And I will see you in the next lecture.

# 269. AWS KMS
# Section: Security, Identity, and Compliance
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-machine-learning-engineer-associate-mla-c01/learn/lecture/45357049
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now let's talk about AWS KMS,
which is a key management service of AWS.
So we've been using it a lot without knowing,
but anytime you hear encryption
when you have an AWS service,
it's most likely going to be KMS encryption.
The aim is that with this KMS service,
AWS is going to manage the encryption keys for us.
And that's great,
because that means that we have less things to do.
So KMS is, of course,
fully integrated with IAM for authorization,
and it gives us very easy ways to control access
to our data if it's encrypted with KMS.
The power of using AWS KMS is that you're able
to audit every single API call made to use your keys
through CloudTrail,
which is something the exam may test you on.
So on top of it,
KMS can be used seamlessly into most AWS services.
So for example, if you wanted to encrypt the data at rest
in an EBS volume, just enable the KMS integration.
Same for S3, same for RDS, same for SSM,
and same for pretty much all the services
that require encryption.
The idea is that with KMS, you can also use it yourself.
And if you have secrets data,
you never ever store them in plain text,
that means just as is.
Especially in your code.
So if you want to use KMS,
you can also use KMS through API calls.
You can use the AWS CLI or the SDK.
And that means that you can encrypt
whatever is a secret for you with a KMS key.
And then these encrypted secrets can be, for example,
stored in your code or in environment variables.
That is a much better pattern.
So now let's talk about the different types
of KMS keys available to you.
So now it's called a KMS key.
By the way, it used to be called
the KMS customer master key, but it was confusing
because there's also the customer managed keys
as we'll see in a second.
So now, we just talk about KMS keys.
So we have two types of KMS keys.
We have the symmetric KMS keys,
and that means there's only one single encrypted key
that is used to encrypt and decrypt data.
And so any service of AWS that is integrated
with KMS will use symmetric keys.
The idea is that when we create or use a KMS symmetric key,
then we never get access to the key itself, okay?
All we do is that we use the KMS API calls
to leverage and use that key.
The second kind of key available on KMS
are called asymmetric keys.
That means that you have two keys.
You have a public key that's used to encrypt data,
and a private key used to decrypt data.
So this is used when you have encrypt/decrypt,
or sign/verify type of operations.
And in that case,
you can download the public key out of KMS,
but you can use access the private key.
You can only use API calls
against to access the private key.
So the use cases for an asymmetric type of key
is when you want the encryption to be done outside
of your AWS cloud by users who cannot
or don't have access to the KMS API key.
In which case they will use the public key
to encrypt the data.
Send it over to you.
And you within your account,
you would use the private key of AWS to decrypt that data.
So within the world of KMS keys,
you have different types of KMS keys.
The first one are AWS owned keys.
They're free, and this is the kind of key you would use
when you use SSE-S3 type of encryption,
or SSC DynamoDB, where you have the option, for example,
that you choose a key owned by DynamoDB.
So these are not really KMS
because you don't really see them,
but they're types of encryption keys within AWS.
Then you have the AWS managed keys, and they're free,
and you will recognize them
because they start with AWS slash and then the service name.
For example, AWS/RDS or AWS/EBS,
or in this example, AWS/DynamoDB.
They're free and you can just use them as you please,
but only from within the service that it's assigned to.
Then you have your own customer managed keys
and their custom keys, and they cost you $1 per month.
And if you want to import them as well, you can import them,
and they cost you $1 per month.
KMS also has a pricing where you're going to pay
for each API call made to the KMS service,
which is about 3 cents per 10,000 API calls.
You also have automatic key rotation.
So if it's an AWS managed KMS key,
then it's automatic every one year.
And if it's a customer managed key,
you can enable automatic rotation and you set the period,
and you can also have on-demand rotation of your key.
And if it's imported KMS key,
then you can only manually rotate it.
And for this, you need to leverage an alias.
So KMS keys are scoped per region.
That means that if you have an EBS volume encrypted
with KMS key in a region, for example, EUS2,
then if you want to copy that to a different region,
we have to do several steps.
First of all, we have to take a snapshot of this EBS volume.
And if we take a snapshot from an encrypted snapshot,
then this snapshot itself will also be encrypted
with the same KMS key.
Then to copy the snapshot to another region,
we need to re-encrypt the snapshot using
a different KMS key.
And this is something AWS will do for you.
But the same KMS key cannot live in two regions.
So now we have an EBS snapshot,
it's encrypted with KMS with a different key,
and it lives in another region.
Now, we restore the snapshot
into its own EBS volume with KMS,
and it's KMS key B into the region AP southeast two.
Now, the other thing we need
to know about is KMS key policies.
So this is to control access to your KMS keys.
It's similar to an S3 bucket policy.
With a difference that if you don't have the KMS key policy
on your KMS key, then no one can access it.
So in that regards, we have two types of KMS key policies.
We have the default one,
and it's created if you don't provide
a specific custom KMS key policy.
And the idea is that the default allows
everyone in your account to access this key.
That means that if you have an IAM policy allowing a user
or role to access this key policy, you're good.
But if you want to have more specific controls over it,
you could use a KMS key policy that is custom.
In which you define the users,
the roles that can access your KMS key.
And you define who can administer the key.
And this is especially helpful
if you want to do cross account access for your KMS key,
because we can authorize another account to use our KMS key.
So when do we use this?
Well, for example,
if we wanted to copy an encrypted snapshots across accounts.
So we create a snapshot encrypted with our own KMS key,
and it's a customer managed key.
It must be that because we need
to attach a custom key policy.
And then we attach a KMS key policy
to authorize for cross account access.
It looks like this.
Then we share the encrypted snapshot
with the target account.
And then in the target account,
we create a copy of the snapshot
and we encrypt it with a different customer managed key
in that target account.
And then we can create a volume from the snapshot
in the target account, and we're done.
So that's a lot of information by KMS,
but let's go into hands-on
to hopefully learn a bit more about it.

# 278. AWS PrivateLink
# Section: Security, Identity, and Compliance
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-machine-learning-engineer-associate-mla-c01/learn/lecture/45357107
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So now let's talk about AWS PrivateLink,
also from the VPC Endpoint Services family.
So how does that work?
Well, say you have a service that you run within AWS,
or say there is a vendor on the Marketplace,
and they run a service on their own account
within their own VPC.
And they want to expose a service to customers of AWS.
So to thousands of VPC, they need to have private access
to that service, to establish a connectivity.
You could, for example, use VPC peering,
but that doesn't scale, and it's not very secure.
What you want is use something else,
and that's something else is a Private Link.
So a Private Link allows you
to connect a service running within your VPC
to other VPCs directly and privately.
So it does not require VPC peering or internet gateway,
because it's from the private network,
or NAT or route tables or anything like this.
So let's go through a diagram.
Say, for example, you are talking to a vendor
on the AWS Marketplace, and they run application service.
So they have their own service that you wanna use
in their own VPC.
And you wanna have access to it from your own VPC
in your own accounts with your own consumer applications.
In that case, you're going to ask your vendor
to do a Private Link.
On their end,
they will have to create a Network Load Balancer
to expose that service.
And on your end,
you will create an Elastic Network Interface,
and then you will establish a Private Link between the two
so that you have private access
to their Network Load Balancer
and therefore to their service.
And all the internet traffic is actually not gonna go
through the public internet,
but it's actually gonna go through your private network.
And so therefore all communications will remain private.
And so for every new customer
that that third party will need,
all they will have to do is to create a new Private Link
for their customers, which is very easy to manage
and way more scalable.
So that's it, I hope you like this lecture,
and I will see you in the next lecture.

So now, let's talk about Amazon CloudWatch.
And the first service I wanna talk about
within CloudWatch is CloudWatch Metrics.
So CloudWatch provides metrics
for every service out there in AWS,
and so, therefore, you can monitor everything
that's happening in your accounts.
And a metric is just a variable you wanna monitor.
For example, for an EC2 instance,
it could be the CPUUtilization, the NetworkIn, and so on.
For Amazon S3, it could be your bucket size and so on.
So metrics belong to namespaces, and, therefore,
they are bucketed in two different namespaces.
You have one namespace per service, basically.
So you have dimensions,
and they are attributes of a metric.
For example, a metric about CPUUtilization
can be related to a specific instance id,
or a specific environment, and so on.
And you have up to 30 dimensions per metric.
So the metrics are time-based,
so, therefore, they must have a timestamp.
And then once you have a lot of metrics,
you can create a CloudWatch dashboard of metrics
so that you can see them all at once in a specific manner.
Also, you can create CloudWatch Custom Metrics.
So instead of relying on the metrics
that are provided by every services in AWS,
you can create your own custom metric.
For example, to extract the memory usage
out of an EC2 instance.
That is a classic use case
of using a CloudWatch Custom Metric.
The other thing you can do with your CloudWatch Metrics
is to stream them outside of CloudWatch.
So the idea is that you want to continuously stream
CloudWatch Metrics to a destination of your choice.
You're gonna get near real-time delivery and low latency.
And that destination is Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose,
and from there, you can send it to anywhere you want.
Or you can also send your CloudWatch Metrics
directly into a third-party service provider,
such as Datadog, Dynatrace, New Relic,
Splunk, Sumo Logic, and so on.

Well, your CloudWatch Metrics are going to be streamed
near real-time into Kinesis Data Firehose,
and you obviously have to set that up for it to work.
And from Kinesis Data Firehose you can, for example,
send them into an Amazon S3 bucket from which you can use
Amazon Athena to analyze your data in Amazon S3,
or you can use Amazon Redshift
to have a data warehousing for your metrics,
or Amazon OpenSearch to build dashboards
from Amazon OpenSearch, or do analytics there.
And you can have the choice to stream
all your metrics for all your namespaces
or to only filter a few namespaces in
so that you only have a subset of your metrics
filtered and sent to Kinesis Data Firehose.
Now let's go have a look in the console.
So when you are in the CloudWatch dashboard
on the left-hand side, there is Metrics,
and you can find all the metrics.

# 281. Amazon CloudWatch - Logs
# Section: Management and Governance
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-machine-learning-engineer-associate-mla-c01/learn/lecture/45357125
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So, now let's talk about CloudWatch Logs.
So CloudWatch Logs is the perfect place
to store your application logs in AWS.
And to do so, you must first define log groups.
They're whatever names you want,
but usually they are representing one of your applications.
Then within a log group, you will have multiple log streams,
and they represent log instances within an application
or specific log files or specific containers that you have
as part of a cluster.
Then you define your log expiration policy.
So you can have the logs re being retained indefinitely
to never expire, or you can choose to expire them
from anywhere between one day to 10 years.
It's also possible to send your CloudWatch Logs
into various destinations.
For example, to export them in batch into Amazon S3
or to stream them into Kinesis Data Streams,
Kinesis Data Firehose, AWS Lambda, Amazon OpenSearch.
All the logs are encrypted by default,
and you can set up your own KMS-based encryption
with your own keys if you wanted to.
So, now what kind of logs data goes into CloudWatch Logs?
Now, what types of logs can go into CloudWatch Logs?
Well, we can send the logs using the SDK
or the CloudWatch Logs Agent
or the CloudWatch Unified Agent.
Now, the CloudWatch Unified Agents send logs to CloudWatch
and so the CloudWatch Log Agent is now sort of deprecated.
You have Elastic Beanstalk, which is used to collect logs
from the application directly into CloudWatch.
ECS will send the logs directly from the containers
into CloudWatch.
Lambda will send logs from the functions themselves.
VPC Flow Logs will send logs specific
to your VPC metadata network traffic.
API Gateway will send all the requests made
to the API Gateway into CloudWatch Logs.
CloudTrail, you can send the logs directly
based on the filter.
And Route53 will log all the DNS queries made
to its service.
So, what if you wanted to query the logs in CloudWatch Logs?
For this, you can use CloudWatch Logs Insights.
So, it's a querying capability within CloudWatch Logs
which allows you to write your query.
You specify the timeframe you want to apply your query to
and then automatically you're going to get a result
as a visualization.
And also, you can view the specific log lines
that's made this visualization.
This visualization can also be exported either
as a result or added to a dashboard
for being able to rerun it whenever you want.
So this is very handy,
and this will allow you to search and analyze log data
within CloudWatch Logs.
So there are lots of simple queries provided
as part of the console for CloudWatch Logs Insights.
For example, you can find the most 25 most recent events,
or you can have a look
at how many events had exceptions or errors in your logs,
or you can look for a specific IP and so on.
So, it provides a purpose-built query language.
All the fields to allow you to build your queries
are automatically detected from CloudWatch Logs,
and then you can filter based on conditions.
You can calculate aggregate statistics,
you can sort events, limit the number of events, and so on.
So as I said, you can save the queries
and also add them to CloudWatch Dashboards.
And you have the capability to query multiple log groups
at a time, even if they are in different accounts.
So remember, CloudWatch Logs Insights is a query engine,
not a real-time engine.
And so as such,
it will only query historical data when you run the query.
So as mentioned,
CloudWatch Logs can be exported into several destinations.
The first one is Amazon S3.
So this is for a batch export to send all your logs
into Amazon S3,
and this export can take up to 12 hours to be completed.
The API call to initiate this export is called
CreateExportTask.
So because this is a batch export,
this is not real-time or near real-time.
Instead, you must use the CloudWatch Logs subscription.
So these allow you to get a real-time stream
of these log events, and you can do processing and analysis.
So, you can send this data into multiple places
such as Kinesis Data Streams, Kinesis Data Firehose,
or Lambda.
And you can specify a subscription filter to say which kind
of log events you want to be delivered to your destination.
So, the subscription filter can send data
into Kinesis Data Streams.
This would be a great choice
if you wanted to use, for example,
the integration with Kinesis Data Firehose,
Kinesis Data Analytics, or Amazon EC2, or Lambda.
You can also directly send it into Kinesis Data Firehose.
From there, you can send it in near real-time fashion
into Amazon S3, or for example,
the OpenSearch Service, or you have Lambda.
So you can write your own custom Lambda function,
or you can use a managed Lambda function that is
sending data in real-time into the OpenSearch Service.
On top of it, thanks to these subscription filters,
it is possible for you to aggregate data
from different CloudWatch Logs into different accounts
and different regions into a common destination
such as the Kinesis Data Stream in one specific accounts.
And then Kinesis Data Firehose.
And then in near real-time into Amazon S3.
So that is very possible,
and that is a way for you to perform log aggregation.
So the nitty gritty of how this works is
that you must use what's called destinations.
So, let's say you have a sender account
and the recipient accounts.
So you create a CloudWatch Log subscription filter,
and then this gets sent into a subscription destination,
which is a virtual representant
of the Kinesis Data Stream in the recipient accounts.
Then you attach a destination access policy
to allow the first account to actually send data
into this destination.
Then you create an IAM role in the recipient account,
which has the permission to send records
into your Kinesis Data Stream,
and you make sure that this role can be assumed
by the first account.
And when you have all these things in place,
then it is possible
for you to send data from CloudWatch Logs
in one account into a destination in another account.
So that's it for this lecture.
I hope you liked it, and I will see you in the next lecture.

# 284. Amazon CloudWatch - Alarms
# Section: Management and Governance
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-machine-learning-engineer-associate-mla-c01/learn/lecture/45357133
# Caption: en_US (manual)

Now let's discuss CloudWatch Alarms.
So alarms, as we know, they're used
to trigger notifications from any metric.
And you can define complex alarms
and on various options such as sampling or doing percentage
or maximum, and so on.
Alarm has three states,
OK, it means that it's not triggered,
INSUFFICIENT_DATA means that there's not enough data
for the alarm to determine a state
and ALARM, which is that your threshold has been breached
and therefore a notification will be sent.
The period is how long you want the alarm
to evaluate for on the metric.
And so it could be very, very short, very, very long.
And it can apply also to high resolution customer metrics.
For example, 10 seconds, 30 seconds,
or multiple of 60 seconds.
Now, alarms have three main targets.
The first one is actions on EC2 instances
such as stopping it, terminating it, rebooting it,
or recovering any instance.
The second one is to trigger an auto-scaling action.
For example, a scale out or a scale in.
And the last one is to send a notification
to the SNS service, for example,
and from the SNS service, we can hook it
to a Lambda function
and have the Lambda function do pretty much anything we want
based on an alarm being breached.
So now let's talk about Composite Alarms,
because we know that CloudWatch Alarms
are on a single metric,
but then if you wanted to have multiple metrics,
you would need to use Composite Alarms.
So because composite alarms are actually monitoring
the states of multiple other alarms,
and these alarms can be each relying
on one different metric.
So the Composite Alarm is the action
of combining all these other alarms together,
and you can use AND or OR conditions
to be able to be very flexible in terms
of the condition you're checking for.
So it's very helpful to reduce alarm noise
because you can create complex Composite Alarms
and saying, for example, if the CPU is high
and the network is high, then don't alert me
because I only wanna know when the CPU is high
and the network is a low, these kind of things.
So let's take an example, we have an EC2 instance,
and we're going to create a composite alarm on top of it.
So therefore we create a first
underlying alarm called the Alarm A,
which is going to monitor the CPU of the EC2 instance.
Then you create Alarm B, which is going to monitor the IOPS
of the EC2 instance,
and then the composite alarm is defined as the junction
of Alarm A and Alarm B.
And therefore, if Alarm A is in alarm
and Alarm B is in alarm,
and this is something we have to define ourselves,
then the Composite Alarm itself will be an alarm
and can trigger, for example, an SNS notification.
So as you can see, you can get quite creative
with the Composite Alarms.
So let's talk about EC2 instance recovery.
So we have the status checks
and we have the instance status check,
which is going to check the EC2 virtual machine.
And we have the system status check,
which is going to check the underlying layer hardware
of our EC2 instance.
And finally, the attached EBS status check,

# 286. AWS X-Ray
# Section: Management and Governance
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-machine-learning-engineer-associate-mla-c01/learn/lecture/45357145
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So, this is to me one of the most
revolutionary services that AWS has to offer
and I think it is currently underutilized.
It's called AWS X-Ray and the exam is really
we want you to know about X-Ray.
I think this is why they ask two questions
because they want people to use it,
and I honestly think people should use X-Ray.
So, when you do debugging production
and I have debugged applications in production in the past,
the good old way, what I call the good old way
is test locally, add log statements everywhere
and redeploying production
and from the logs try to figure out
what is breaking, what is happening.
It's really painful.
It's not best practices.
Obviously, there are better ways of doing things.
I'm just oversimplifying things here, but you get the idea.
Debugging production is not fun.
And then, if you log stuff,
if you have different applications,
if you log from different applications to CloudWatch
then you know they all have different formats
and it's really hard to centralize insights.
And navigating CloudWatch logs is gonna be hard.
And analytics on top of it, it's going to be hard.
So, if you have a monolith, just one huge application
doing everything is sort of easy to debug,
but if you have distributed services
you're running a hundred microservices in your LS accounts,
it becomes a nightmare.
It's really, really hard to debug what's happening
because they all talk to each other, right?
So, there's no common view of your entire architecture,
your entire service map, et cetera.
So, here comes AWS X-Ray.
So, X-ray is going to give you a visual analysis
of your application.
So, this is what we're going to do in the hands-on.
We'll see that basically as a client doing a request
to our application we will see how many
of these requests fail or don't fail.
And then, from the application we'll see what it does.
So, it will call other IPs, it will call SNS
it will call a DynamoDB Table.
And so, as you can see, we'll be able to trace exactly,
visually what happens when we talk to our EC2 instance.
And so, you know from this graph
if I ask you where do you think
that little orange or yellow error comes from?
Well, is it coming from this?
No, is it coming from SNS?
No, it is coming from my DynamoDB Table.
You can see it visually.
And so, that's the whole power of tracing.
Obviously, you can do more, but you start getting the idea.
In terms of X-ray advantages, there's many.
You can troubleshoot the performance
of your application and identify bottlenecks.
You can understand the dependencies
in your microservice architecture
because you can visually see what is happening
and how all your microservices interact with one another.
We can pinpoint then which service is giving us issues.
We can understand how each request is behaving
and then find errors and exception based on the request.
We can answer questions such as, are we meeting time SLA
in terms of latency or time to process a request?
And we can understand which service
really slows down, throttles us.
Finally, we can know which users are impacted
by our errors if we wanted to.
So, X-ray has a lot of compatibility.
It's compatible with AWS Lambda, Beanstalk,
ECS, ELBs, API gateway, and EC2 instances
or any application server really,
even something you have on premise.
So, they really made X-Ray try to be as wide as possible
and as applicable as to any application they can.
So, X-Ray, how does it work?
Well, it leverages something called tracing.
And tracing is an end to a way
to basically follow a request.
So, when I make a request to, for example,
my application server, each component that will deal
with a request that could be my database,
that could be my gateway, my load balancer,
my application server.
Each component dealing with that request
will add its own trace, and so, the trace will be made
of segments and segments can be made of sub segments.
And the idea is that we can also add annotations
to traces to provide extra information around what happened.
So, when all these things are together,
you have the ability to trace every request
or a simple request.
So, you say I only want to get a percentage
of the total request or maybe five requests per minutes.
In terms of security, there is IAM authorization
and you can use KMS for encryption at rest.
So, once you get all these traces,
basically, X-Ray provides its magic
and provide this nice little graph that I showed you before.
Now, how do you enable X-Ray?
Well, you have two ways
and I think this is what the exam will ask you about.
So, you need to be very careful here.
Your code can be Java, Python, Go, Node.js and .Net
and it must import the AWS SDK.
You need very little code modification,
but you still need to do some code modification.
And then, the application SDK,
the X-Ray SDK, will then capture the calls
to the AWS services, the HTTP and HTTPS request
and the database calls for MySQL, PostgreSQL and DynamoDB.
It can also capture queue calls and so on.
Now, the second thing we have to do
once we've modified our code is to install the X-Ray daemon
or to enable the X-Ray AWS integration.
So, if we run on a machine, on-premise server
or EC2 instance, we need to install the daemon.
And the daemon is basically a little program that works
as a low level UDP packet interceptor.
It can be running on Linux, Windows, and Mac.
And so, you have to install it on your machine.
If you use AWS Lambda or other services
that already have integration with X-Ray
then they will run the daemon for you
and you don't have to worry about it.
Now, each application also must have the IAM rights
to write data to X-Ray.
So, a very common question is, hey, my X-Ray application
works on my computer when I test locally,
but doesn't work on my EC2 machine, why?
Well, the answer is probably because on your machine
you're running the X-Ray daemon,
but when you deploy to your EC2 instance,
it's not running the X-Ray daemon,
and therefore, X-Ray doesn't see your calls.
Now, to make it really crystal clear
here is an EC2 instance and you need to have
your application code on top of it.
And so, your code again needs to be modified
to import the AWS X-Ray SDK, and then it will send
its traces to the X-Ray daemon running the machine.
So, as you can see, you also need to run the X-Ray daemon
and that X-Ray daemon will send a batch
every one second to AWS X-Ray.
So, X-Ray does some magic.
And so, to update this graph, how does that work?
X-Ray will collect all the data
from all the different services sending traces,
and then, the service map will be computed magically
from all the segments and the traces.
And so, that's a really cool thing.
X-ray is graphical, so even non-technical people
can help troubleshoot.
Talking about trouble shooting,
what if X-Ray is not working on EC2?
As I said, you need to ensure that the IAM role
has the proper permission and you need to ensure
that the EC2 instance is indeed running the X-Ray Daemon.
If you want to run it on Lambda,
it's a little bit different.
For it, you need to ensure that the Lambda
has an IAM execution role with proper policy.
And I know we haven't seen what Lambda is,
but it's just a question you may get.
So, you need to make sure that Lambda has a proper IAM role
that's expected and then you need to ensure
that the X-Ray code is imported.
And finally, that you have activated the active
tracing Lambda option on X-Ray,
but we'll see this in the Lambda section as well.
So, that's it for the overview of X-Ray, a little taster.
In the next lecture, we're just going to run
the several apps on X-Ray to get a better feeling
of how it works.
So, see you in the next lecture.

# 294. CloudWatch vs. CloudTrail vs. Config
# Section: Management and Governance
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-machine-learning-engineer-associate-mla-c01/learn/lecture/45357169
# Caption: en_US (manual)

So one very popular exam question
is to make the distinction
between CloudWatch, CloudTrail, and Config.
Now thankfully, thanks to the hands-on,
hopefully you know exactly what are the differences are.
It's pretty obvious in my opinion,
but it's never too bad
to go through an example and see them.
So CloudWatch is for performance metrics,
metrics, CPU, network, and to create dashboards.
You can also get events and alerts,
and finally, we have a log aggregation and analysis tool
if we wanted to.
So CloudWatch, I think we're all pretty familiar with it,
this already.
Now, CloudTrail could be new to you,
but basically it's to record API calls
made within your account by everyone and everything,
and you can define some trails for specific resources,
so you can get more information on EC2 only,
and it's a global service.
Now finally, Config is to record configuration changes
and to evaluate resources configuration
against compliance rules.
Finally, you're going to get a timeline
of changes and compliance with its nice UI.
So, I think they're a very distinctive service
I don't think there's any confusion,
but let's go through an Elastic Load Balancer
to see how each of these service
can help you understand what is happening to your ELB.
So CloudWatch can monitor
the number of incoming connections,
can visualize number of error codes
as a percentage over time,
and maybe we can have a dashboard
to get an idea of the load balancer performance,
maybe we can have a,
even make it a global dashboard
if you have multiple load balancers
for a global application.
Now, Config, why would we use Config on the ELB?
Well, maybe you wanna track
the security group rules for the load balancer,
making sure no-one does anything fishy or changes anything,
maybe you want to change also a track
that configuration changes for the load balancer itself,
to see if anyone modifies the SSL certificate,
or et cetera, et cetera.
We also maybe have a rule to say,
oh there's always should be an SSL certificate
assigned to the load balancer,
and maybe we should never allow
non-encrypted traffic into the load balancer,
that could be two different compliance rules
that you put into Config.
Finally, CloudTrail will be to track who made any changes
to the load balancer with API calls.
So, in case someone changes the security group rules
or someone changes the SSL certificate,
or removes it, or whatever,
then CloudTrail will be how we know who made these changes.
So all these tools are complementary when you think about it
and when you understand that,
how they're used for a load balancer,
which I think is a great example,
then you are going to rock any questions
asked for you at the exam.
So I hope that makes sense,
and I will see you in the next lecture.

You would use AWS Budgets
if you wanted to create a budget based on actual charges
or future estimated charges
and send alarms whenever your cost will exceed your budgets.
So you have four types of budgets you can set
in the budget console.
You can use usage, cost, reservation and savings plan,
and we'll see them in a second.
In case of signing a budget for a reserve instance,
you can track utilization of your reserve instances overall
and it supports RIs for different services
such as EC2, ElastiCache, RDS, and Redshift.
You can set up to five notifications per budgets
and you can filter your budget by many different options
such as service, linked account, tag, purchase options,
and so on.
So that means that you get a lot of options,
actually the same as Cost Explorer,
and so that makes budgets something that is going
to be a lot more granular, a lot more flexible
when it comes to tracking your cost
and setting up alarms than, for example,
your billing alarms.
So the first two budgets are going to be free
and then you're going to pay 2 cents per day per budget.
So now let's go have a look in the console
to see how budgets work.

But as we can see, we have two
on security that must be looked at.
So it turns out that one of my bucket
is actually allowing a global access.
So I need to verify it and make sure it's correct.
And as you can see, 29 of my 60 security group rules

I get prompted to upgrade my support plan

Operational excellence, again, access to nothing.
