# 300. AWS Tools for Responsible AI
# Section: Machine Learning Best Practices
# https://ua.udemy.com/course/aws-certified-machine-learning-engineer-associate-mla-c01/learn/lecture/57864813
# Caption: en_US (auto)

Let's talk about classical machine learning and generative AI system architecture and
some best practices surrounding it in this section.
Let's start with the concept of responsible AI.
What does that mean?
So it's a term you hear a lot, but concretely there are many dimensions to it that you need
to think about when you're deploying these systems and designing them.
One is fairness.
You know, is it behaving in a fair manner to people?
Are there inherent biases to your model that might cause decisions that are biased in one
way or another and aren't fair to certain classes of people?
That's the big one, right? Explainability.
And this is a hard thing with AI.
Can I actually explain why it made the decision it did?
Why it produced the output that it did?
This is very hard to do with these giant large language models where the internals are often
quite opaque, but tools are emerging to help us explain that a little bit better.
And in the more deterministic field of classical machine learning, this gets a little bit easier
with metrics like SHAP.
Privacy and security.
Are we actually making sure that we're filtering out personally identifiable information or
sensitive information or confidential information in this system or not? Safety.
Am I telling people to do bad things that might cause harm?
That would be bad.
That would be irresponsible, right?
So that's not responsible AI.
Controllability.
Can I control how this model is behaving?
You know, it was in the news at one point that some frontier models were going out and
hacking companies because they escaped their sandbox.
That is not responsible AI.
That is a AI that went out of control.
So that's another dimension of responsible AI.
Veracity and robustness. Is it lying?
You know, is it hallucinating a lot?
We can measure these things and compare its output to ground truth to figure out if it's
actually telling the truth or not and how robust it is to different types of prompts
and potentially prompt attacks.
Governance is this thing compliant with all the regulations it needs to comply with.
You know, in different jurisdictions, there may be different restrictions on what your
model can and cannot do or be used for or used by whom.
And we need to comply with that.
Transparency, just giving you more information about why it gave you the answer that it did.
So am I being transparent about the reasoning steps that it took about the sources that
it consulted about its reasoning process and giving you a final result and whether or not
I can trust the sources of the information that was behind it?
That's all transparency.
And it's a big challenge with generative AI.
So how do I actually measure responsibility?
That's kind of a big question, right?
With traditional or classical ML, it's actually fairly straightforward.
So I have a bunch of training data that I'm training a model with, right?
And I'm going to have bias and fairness metrics that I can use to evaluate that training data.
So I can measure before I do anything with that data before I train a model at all, whether
or not there's any bias baked into that data that I need to account for somehow.
And you know, there's different ways of accounting for bias that we can talk about in machine
learning and different ways of measuring that.
But it's a pretty straightforward thing, right?
And we can just check the data quality as well, making sure we don't have missing fields
or, you know, inconsistent labels or, you know, classifications or columns that shouldn't be there.
Things like that.
Once we've cleaned our data and we're sure that it doesn't have any bias, and these are
easy things to measure, we can train our model with it.
And hopefully it gives you something good.
Once we have a trained model, though, we need to explain and evaluate it.
So those are other dimensions of our responsible AI, right?
So we have tools like SHAP that can be used to measure feature attribution.
So the idea there is that you can actually use that to attribute outputs to the training
features that were used to generate that output.
That's actually turns out to be a fairly straightforward thing to do.
So that gives you some explainability.
And of course, you can evaluate that model in any number of ways, usually by just comparing
its predicted outputs to known good outputs, right?
So MAE, RMSE, whatever it is.
We can also use tools like MLflow combined with SageMaker AI to track those experiments
and model metrics and artifacts for reproducibility and whatnot.
So MLflow, again, enters the equation here as sort of a replacement for SageMaker technologies
that have been deprecated.
It might be a good idea to have a human in the loop at this point.
So if there is any real consequences or high stakes to this model, you probably want a
human review of that before you actually deploy it to the world.
And at that point, once a human's happy, once your metrics are happy, deploy it and continue to measure it.
So once it's in production, your job is not done.
You can't just fire and forget.
You're going to use tools like CloudWatch and QuickSight and various AWS monitoring
solutions to make sure that this continues to behave the way that you expect over time.
And there used to be a whole suite of built-in tools with SageMaker, SageMaker Clarify, Model
Monitor, A2I, and Role Manager, but these are all on maintenance mode now.
So the modern way of enforcing responsible AI is now using the approaches shown on this slide.
With generative AI, things are a little bit different.
There's a different set of tools you might use due to the non-deterministic manner of
how generative AI operates.
And Amazon Bedrock Model Evaluations is going to be the main thing you need to know about
in that context.
So I'm going to have some sort of evaluation data set of prompts and expected responses,
and then Bedrock Model Evaluations can use that to measure the performance of my generative
AI model in a way that's a little bit more qualitative.
So we can't just do straight up string matching with generative AI.
We have to evaluate it against some sort of a threshold.
So assess the correctness, relevance, safety, bias in some manner using model evaluations.
And there are different ways of doing that.
There are metrics that we can use that are just straight up math.
We can have humans in the loop for doing that evaluation, or we can use another model as
the judge of this model with the LLM as a judge pattern.
At runtime, we also need guardrails to enforce safety and policy on every individual request.
So we can evaluate the model itself, but that's not enough.
We still need to make sure that every prompt that's coming in is being checked against
guardrails and every output coming out of our model is also being checked against guardrails
to ensure we're not doing anything that's letting personal information through or unsafe
advice from going through.
So that's going to be applied at runtime, independent of our evaluations as well.
So evaluations of your model using Bedrock Model Evaluations, or whatever you choose
to use, will measure the behavior of your model, but you still need guardrails to enforce runtime policy.
You need both for responsible AI.
One does not replace the other.
They are complementary.
And you need to expect that the world is going to change around you.
So as your models and your prompts change, as your data changes, as user behavior changes,
or the context your application is in changes, then these metrics are going to change as well.
So you need to keep monitoring this stuff in production.
You can't just measure it once and forget about it.
And you can also use tools, by the way, like Amazon Macie to continue monitoring the introduction
of sensitive data in S3 that might be filtering into your training data set over time.
So vigilance is key here.
You need to keep that monitoring running when you're in production forever.
You need to be monitoring for sensitive data forever.
You need to be running these guardrails forever.
It's not just a one-off thing.
